L A L E Y E N D A D E L P E Q U E Ñ O B R U J O
En los confines más ardientes del reino nació el protagonista de
nuestra historia. Un niño de ojos azules y cabellos dorados. . . que el
tiempo le robaría. Desde su más tierna infancia, evocaba singularidad.
Era alguien peculiar, y jamás intentó contentar a nadie, lo cual bastó
para que los demás habitantes le mirasen con desconfianza. Sin em-
bargo, él se mantuvo fiel a sus principios y a su forma de pensar. Eso
le dio libertad. . . Pero también lo arrojó al ostracismo. Aunque eso ya
es otra historia.
Este infante fue afortunado al tener dos Guardianes que velaron
por él, y por su hermano, Sir David, durante toda su vida. Estos
Guardianes eran conocidos por aquellas tierras como Don Juan Carlos,
el Zapatero Agreste, y Doña Inmaculada, la Guardiana de la Constancia.
La vida no era fácil, y numerosos conflictos acontecieron durante aquel-
los años: periodos de escasez, disputas con habitantes del reino, plagas,
enfermedades. . . Pero todo eso forjó el carácter del pequeño brujo, al
que sus Guardianes protegieron y educaron por encima de cualquier
adversidad. En un reino donde imperaban el egoísmo, la mentira y el
interés era raro encontrar Guardianes con tales principios férreos. No
vivieron en opulencia, pero tampoco en escasez. Simplemente, nuestro
protagonista creció con la certeza de que todo en la vida había que
ganárselo. Aprendió a salvaguardar cada recurso, y fue educado en
humildad, sacrificio, resiliencia, esfuerzo y constancia. Unos valores
que lo distinguieron durante su educación y que, sin duda, perdurarán
en él hasta el fin de sus días. En numerosas ocasiones, el pequeño
brujo afirmó que prefería vivir en el ostracismo social antes que ser un
corderito más del rebaño de ignorantes del reino. Esta personalidad
marcada se la debe a sus Guardianes. Es lo más valioso que posee, más
allá incluso de la materia gris de su cerebro.
Salvaguardando a los Guardianes, hubo dos Centinelas que se
dedicaron con total devoción y generosidad a su crianza. Su altruismo
fue tal que, ni en mil vidas, el pequeño brujo podría agradecerles
todo lo que hicieron por él. Estos Centinelas vivieron para ayudar. . .
sin pedir jamás nada a cambio. Por aquel reino eran conocidos como
Maese Currito, el Alquimista Benevolente, y Doña Rosario, la Costur-
era del Sosiego. Nunca se tuvo constancia de almas tan cándidas y
amables. A pesar de los conflictos armados que arrasaron el reino, de
las hambrunas severas y de enfermedades trágicas, nunca perdieron la
sonrisa. Fueron capaces de vivir en paz y de ayudar a todo aquel que
lo pidiera, aunque muchos se merecieran ser ejecutados entre terribles
sufrimientos. Dos seres de luz para un reino de tinieblas.
iii


iv
Nuestro protagonista fue creciendo, forjando su carácter entre se-
mejantes que nunca le quisieron. Realmente, solo tenía a sus Centinelas
y a sus Guardianes. En un reino donde los mozos acudían a tabernas
entregados a los placeres hedonistas, propio de seres con alma de
rebaño, él se apartaba. Nunca fue lo suyo. Se recluyó en sus propias
aficiones. Le daba igual estar solo, siempre fue fiel a su manera de ver
la vida. No estaba hecho para ser una caricatura de un molde vacío.
Quería algo más. Y decidió emprender el sendero del brujo.
Un camino aciago y difícil que solo alguien como él podía recorrer.
Quería cazar monstruos. Emprender aventuras. Hacer aquello que
era necesario para todos los habitantes del reino, pero que casi nadie
se atrevía a hacer. Un trabajo duro, arriesgado, sin seguridad, mal
pagado y sin reconocimiento. . . pero vital para la evolución de la
sociedad. Los grandes reyes destinaban escasos recursos a la formación
de nuevos brujos. Preferían invertirlos en la manipulación del pueblo.
No querían habitantes sabios, sino borregos obedientes. A pesar de las
adversidades, nuestro protagonista tenía un objetivo, y se dispuso a
cumplirlo. Comenzó su entrenamiento.
Afortunadamente, no recorrió ese camino solo. A su lado, en todo
momento, estuvo su Hermano de Acero, su Compañero de Armas: Sir
Daniel. Sin llegar al ostracismo del protagonista, era un caballero que
tampoco comulgaba con las corrientes del reino. Emprendieron, sin
saberlo, el sendero del brujo el mismo día. Un camino que les conduciría
a incontables aventuras por Novigrado, Velen y las Islas Skellige en
busca de Leshens, Demonibestias y Wyvernos, entre otros seres de
dudosa moral alejados de simples monstruos. Desde aquel primer
momento, en que ambos ayudaron a categorizar las herramientas de
los brujos oficiales, fueron como uña y carne. Aprendieron juntos el
oficio, y caminaron de la mano hasta el final. Mientras la mayoría de
sus semejantes vivía entre festines de alcohol y opio, ellos se recluían en
su morada, disfrutando de sus propios juegos. Les fascinaba lo oculto.
Siempre lo hizo. Tenían sus costumbres y jamás las traicionaron.
Tal fue la fama de ambos aprendices de brujo que, incluso, algunos
en el reino llegaron a insinuar que aquella hermandad era algo más.
Simples habladurías de callejón. Su vínculo fue siempre fraternal, desde
el respeto, y eso lo puede confirmar la Dama de Sir Daniel: Lady
Inmaculada. Ella se integró en el grupo de camaradas, lo que hizo que
Sir Daniel relegara a nuestro protagonista a un nuevo ostracismo latente.
Él no le guardó rencor. Sabía que la hermandad, aunque recorriesen
sendas distintas, viviría hasta el último aliento.
Si este relato está siendo escrito, es porque el pequeño brujo ha
conseguido completar la formación más elevada del entrenamiento. Y
esto no habría sido posible sin su mentor: Maese Jesús, el Custodio del
Manuscrito. En los niveles más avanzados de la caza de monstruos,
existen técnicas arcanas que deben dominarse para poder enfrentarlos.


v
Conocimiento complejo, que requiere años de experiencia. Como eru-
dito, su maestro se esforzó en transmitirle estas artes ocultas. Fueron
años de trabajo para ambos, con adversidades y contratiempos, pero
al final lograron terminar este Grimorio. Un compendio de nuevas
habilidades con las que buscan expandir el saber del noble arte de la
caza de monstruos.
La formación tuvo lugar en un anciano castillo, oculto en la ladera
de la montaña más alta del reino. Varios eruditos lo habitaban. Algunos,
como Sir Luis Javier o Sir Francisco Ortuño, deben ser nombrados
por las ayudas que ofrecieron al protagonista cuando él las solicitó.
Además, una figura muy especial en aquel castillo fue Maese Paco
Illeras. Aunque no era versado en la caza de monstruos, todos los mae-
stros le debían gratitud, pues se encargaba de gestionar herramientas
y materiales para todos. Finalmente, durante la formación, el mayor
de los eruditos, el Archimago Julio Ortega, falleció. Cualquiera que
haya cruzado su camino con él sabrá que era alguien que dejaba huella.
Sabiduría y tolerancia fueron sus virtudes más preciadas, y su mensaje
caló hondo en todo el círculo de sabios.
El camino hasta sellar este Grimorio no fue fácil, pero el brujo se
mantuvo firme y perseverante, como siempre. Su devoción y entrega
han sido su punta de lanza. Se mantuvo fiel a los principios ya narrados:
aprender de cada experiencia y encontrar lo valioso en cada vivencia.
Ser como él implica librar batallas constantes contra el mundo. Y, en
medio de esa tormenta, su corazón se ablandó cuando estrechó lazos
con la niña pequeña de la familia: la Hija de la Eterna Sonrisa, Lady
Silvia. Cada lucha perdida, cada afrenta, cada sombra. . . se deshacía
al volver al refugio, y verla a ella. No era su hija, pero juntos crearon
un lazo difícil de romper. El mayor deseo del brujo es que esa sonrisa
nunca se apague, y que ella —y los demás infantes del linaje— caminen
en paz hacia el destino que decidan explorar.
Ahora que este Grimorio está completo y sellado, el futuro del
pequeño brujo es una hoja en blanco. El relato de cómo se convirtió
en brujo ya está escrito. . . pero las siguientes batallas están por llegar.
Aún habrá monstruos. Y peligros. Pero si algo puede asegurarse, es
que él los enfrentará como ha hecho siempre: sin rendirse.
El pequeño brujo da las gracias.
A los pocos que le tendieron la mano. . .
Y a los muchos que no.
Porque incluso de ellos aprendió.
Y si ha llegado hasta aquí, es por todos.


A B S T R A C T
One field that has gained significant importance in recent times is
bioinformatics, which involves the analysis of large volumes of bio-
logical data using high-performance computing devices. One of the
primary challenges in bioinformatics is to identify and extract the in-
formation underlying the data that is most relevant, while eliminating
information that could potentially distort the model generated to study
new samples. It is essential to perform this task in a rigorous manner
to ensure the data are processed correctly. While data processing in-
volves multiple stages, the stage responsible for obtaining the subset of
features that best represents the original dataset is known as feature
selection. This is the focus of the present doctoral thesis.
Over the years, there have been numerous attempts to improve the
effectiveness and efficiency of feature selection procedures. The aim
of these attempts has been to obtain better solutions while reducing
resource consumption. However, there is still room for further improve-
ment and study of these procedures with both premises in mind. This
thesis makes contributions in this direction.
When analyzing high-dimensional data in bioinformatics tasks, it is
essential to configure the hyperparameters that regulate these proce-
dures with precision and care. While there is a general consensus in
the literature on how to adjust them properly, some areas have not
been fully explored in the context of this type of problem. This ques-
tion is of great interest, as the chapters show. The effectiveness and
efficiency of a procedure are both dependent on the adjustment of
hyperparameters. In a world in which resources are increasingly scarce,
it is vital to develop efficient procedures to protect the environment.
High-performance systems have been used to considerably speed up
processing, reducing both execution time and energy consumption.
vii


R E S U M E N
Una disciplina que ha adquirido gran relevancia a día de hoy es la
bioinformática, en la que grandes volumenes de datos biológicos son
analizados utilizando dispositivos informáticos con una alta capacidad
computacional. Una de las cuestiones clave en bioinformática es ex-
traer aquella información subyacente a los datos que resulta realmente
relevante, eliminando aquella que pueda distorsionar el modelo ge-
nerado para estudiar nuevas muestras. Esta tarea se debe realizar de
manera rigurosa para procesar los datos adecuadamente. Aunque el
procesamiento de los datos está formado por varias etapas, aquella que
se encarga de obtener el subconjunto de características que mejor repre-
sente al dataset original es conocida como selección de características,
y es aquí donde se enmarca la presente tesis doctoral.
A lo largo de los años, se han ido realizando numeros intentos para
mejorar la eficacia y la eficiencia de los procedimentos de selección de
características, con el objetivo de obtener mejores soluciones reduciendo
el consumo de recursos. Sin embargo, todavía existe margen para seguir
mejorando y estudiando estos procedimientos con ambas premisas en
mente, por lo que las aportaciones realizadas en esta tesis van en esta
dirección.
A la hora de analizar datos de alta diminsionalidad en tareas de bioin-
formática, es esencial configurar minuciosamente los hiperparámetros
que regulan estos procedimientos. Aunque en la literatura existe, en
mayor o menor medida, cierto consenso acerca de cómo ajustarlos
adecuadamente, algunos de ellos no han sido explorados de manera
exhaustiva en este tipo de problemas. Esta cuestión es realmente in-
teresante porque, tal y como se analiza a lo largo de los capítulos, no
solo la eficacia del procedimento está condicionada por el ajuste de los
hiperparámentros, sino también la eficiencia. En un mundo donde el
consumo de recursos aumenta cada año, es crucial desarollar proce-
dimientos eficientes para así cuidar el medio ambiente. En este sentido,
las capacidades computacionales de los sistemas de alto rendimiento
han sido utilizadas para acelerar consideralemente el procesamiento,
logrando así reducir tanto el tiempo de ejecución como la energía
consumida.

acquired greater relevance over the years is bioinformatics because
of its relevance to health issues. Bioinformatics focuses on the study

Biological datasets are obtained by extracting data from a part of a

commonly referred to as ML pipeline. ML, described in Section 1.1, can

1.1
machine learning pipeline
As previously mentioned, data analysis is conducted using the ML
pipeline, as illustrated in Figure 1.1. Since data are extracted from the
original source, until the final model is built, a sequence of steps is
necessary for the whole study to be performed in an adequate and
statistically robust manner. Throughout this section, each phase is
briefly detailed to locate this thesis.
1.1.1
Data ingestion
The first phase, commonly known as data ingestion [9, 10], is respon-
sible for gathering the raw data from the source. In some cases, this
phase may also include feature extraction, which is discussed later in
Section 1.1.2. Because the processing of datasets is built sequentially,
it is critical that each phase is conducted in a proper and exhaustive
manner. Otherwise, the subsequent phases of the pipeline would be
greatly disturbed, resulting in an erroneous analysis. As data ingestion
is responsible for collecting the original information, the process must
be accomplished thoroughly to obtain the highest possible quality data.
Although different types of data ingestion can be found, most of them
are based, to a greater or lesser extent, on the two described below:
• Batch data ingestion. Data are gathered from one or multiple
sources in different batches. It is recommended for processing
large volumes of data that do not involve real-time processing.
Typically, these data are collected at specific time intervals.
• Real-time data ingestion. Here, data are stored as soon as they are
generated, which is usually done using sensors, IoT devices, social
IoT: Internet of
Things
media feeds, etc. Typically, data are processed in microbatches or
individually, which requires processors with a low latency. Data
collection in different fields of bioinformatics is usually of this
type because external devices, such as electrodes or technological
laboratory instruments, are commonly used.

1.1.2
Feature extraction
Once data have been gathered from one or various sources, they are
in raw format. Although it is possible that an ML model can analyze
them in this format in some cases, it is very common that a process of
creation of the final dataset is needed. A dataset is a set of information,
numerical or alphabetical, arranged in rows and columns, i.e., a matrix.
The rows are known as samples, and the columns as features, attributes,
or genes, depending on the field of study. In this sense, the purpose of
the feature extraction phase is to convert the raw data into a dataset that
the ML model can understand adequately.
In short, the feature extraction process creates valuable information from
raw data by reformatting, combining, or transforming the original
features into ones that the ML model can analyze to improve its ef-
fectiveness. Therefore, this process is also known as feature engineering
because it inherently creates new features from those that comprise the
raw data. There are many feature extraction techniques, but their analysis
is beyond the scope of this doctoral thesis. Nevertheless, studies such
as [11–13] can be consulted for more information on this topic.
1.1.3
Data pre-processing
Once the two previous phases have been fulfilled, any ML procedure
could tackle the dataset analysis. However, the data pre-processing stage
is really interesting to address problems such as missing values, outliers,
or data inconsistency that may disturb the final model. Specifically, as
illustrated in Figure 1.1, this stage is in turn constituted by successive
sub-steps that allow proper data preparation.
1.1.3.1
Data cleaning
It is quite common to find samples that differ from the numerical
trend of the samples inside a dataset, abruptly deviating from the
mean. These samples are considered outliers and should be removed
to improve the quality of the data. Otherwise, they would cause errors
in the generation of the learning model, leading to a misunderstanding
of the actual information underlying the data. Thus, it is necessary to
define a good strategy for detecting outliers to avoid biased data.


8
1 introduction
1.1.3.2
Data integration
This step is optional and its application depends on the kind of data to
be used, since its objective is to group different datasets into a single
one. Some examples in which this integration is necessary are described
below:
• Schema integration. Schema from different sources may not be
compatible. Consider two datasets R and S, in which source id is
represented as source_id in R and as s_id in S. They represent the
same variable but have different names, which leads to integration
problems. Detecting and resolving such issues is very important
to have a coherent dataset.
• Data value conflicts. The values, metrics, or representations of
the same data may be different depending on the dataset. For
example, suppose a dataset R in which weight is represented in
kilograms and another dataset S that represents it in grams. To
resolve this, data representations should be made consistent and
conversions should be performed accordingly.
• Redundant data. Duplicate attributes or tuples may occur as a
result of integrating data from various sources. This may also lead
to inconsistencies, which should be reduced by careful integration
of data from multiple sources.
1.1.3.3
Data scaling
It is quite common that different features have values on a different
scale, which could lead to an erroneous calculation of the distance
between different samples, for example. Features with a larger scale
would have greater relevance than those with a smaller scale, causing
distortion in the measurements. In this context, the concept of data
normalization arises, in which each column of the dataset (feature)
is normalized independently in a given range. The most common
approach is to use the range [0, 1], although it is not recommended
when data are not free of outliers. As discussed in Section 1.1.3.1,
outlier removal is a sensitive task and it is difficult to discern whether
a sample is an outlier or not.


1.1 machine learning pipeline

1.1.4
Feature selection
Now, the dataset is properly prepared for analysis, leading to the FS
phase whose objective is to address the curse of dimensionality problem.
This process is also known as variable selection, attribute selection, data
reduction, or variable subset selection. Although with data pre-processing,
the size of the data could have been reduced, it is common that they
still consist of thousands of features. Therefore, the FS phase, whose
goal is basically to obtain the subset of features that best represents the
original dataset, is crucial. The procedures developed in this doctoral
thesis are framed in this fourth stage of the ML pipeline, so Section 1.2
details it more extensively.
1.1.5
Model selection
The next step is to choose the final ML model to learn the information
underlying the data correctly. In this context, the nature of the problem
addressed (classification, regression, or clustering) must be consid-
ered to determine the most appropriate model, which is trained using
only the dataset’s features obtained in the previous step. Besides, it is
necessary to regulate the behavior of the chosen model through its hy-
perparameters, which are also usually adjusted at this stage. However,
although it is not usual, the model could not use any hyperparameter.
1.1.6
Model generation
Once the relevant features of the dataset have been selected and the
model has been chosen, a subset of the data, called the training data,
is used, along with a set of model hyperparameters and a training
algorithm to train the model to learn the training data. Usually, the
training data are split again into training and validation data to avoid
the overfitting problem [14], which occurs when the model fits too
closely to the training data and is unable to generalize the underlying
information in the data, negatively affecting the model’s performance.


10
1 introduction
1.1.7
Model validation
After obtaining the ML model it is necessary to validate its efficacy.
Thus, the remaining samples not used in the training phase (the test
dataset) are used to perform this task. In addition, depending on the
type of problem, different metrics could be employed, such as accuracy,
F1-score, or Kappa index.
1.1.8
Model deployment
Finally, after verifying that the trained model works correctly, it could
be deployed locally or in the cloud using platforms such as Amazon
Web Services, Azure, or Google Cloud Platform.
1.2
feature selection
As discussed in the previous section, FS forms the fourth step of the ML
pipeline and is the focus of this thesis. Basically, the ultimate purpose
of any FS technique is the detection of relevant features that help to
discover the knowledge underlying the data, eliminating those features
that are considered noise, redundant, or irrelevant. These three terms
can be defined as follows:
• A noisy feature is one that disturbs the subsequent analysis phase
causing the model to not learn correctly.
• A feature is considered redundant when it does not give more
information than the currently selected features.
• A feature is irrelevant when it does not provide useful informa-
tion.
FS becomes especially relevant when analyzing high-dimensional data,
since the thousands or tens of thousands of features that conform
them preclude checking all possible combinations of subset of fea-
tures. Furthermore, if no FS technique is applied, the analysis of high-
dimensional datasets would present several critical problems. The
first is known as the overfitting problem, previously mentioned in
Section 1.1.6. The second problem is related to the large amount of


1.2 feature selection
11
memory required to store data. High-dimensional datasets are usually
megabytes or gigabytes in size, resulting memory storage requirements
and computational costs to increase exponentially. Finally, the execu-
tion time required to analyze the data, with the consequent energy
consumption, would be exorbitant. Thus, it becomes necessary to em-
ploy FS techniques to choose the subset of features that best represents
the original dataset.
Over the years, different approaches to solving FS problems have been
presented [15, 16]. However, two have become the winning horses
when this problem is addressed: wrapper and filter approaches. The
former search for the best subset of features along with an induction
algorithm that evaluates each possible solution to the problem. On
the contrary, filter approaches select features using a preprocessing
step, before processing the data. Finally, it is interesting to comment on
embedded methods [17], which try to combine the benefits of wrappers
and filters. In them, FS is integrated as part of the learning algorithm.
1.2.1
Filter methods
The main characteristic of filter methods is that they select features
independently of the induction algorithm used later to process the
data, so one of their great advantages is that they are computationally
less demanding than wrapper methods. Filters perform a ranking of
the different features according to their relevance, which is calculated
through statistical metrics such as Pearson’s correlation, LDA, ANOVA,
LDA: Fisher’s
Linear Discriminant
Analysis
ANOVA: ANalysis
Of VAriance
Chi-square, Wilcoxon-Mann-Whitney test, or mutual information. Also,
filters are usually classified into two types: univariate and multivariate
[18]. In the univariate scheme, each feature is ranked individually re-
gardless of other features, while the multivariate scheme ranks multiple
features in a batch way.
Nonetheless, it should be noted that filters have the great disadvantage
of bias since features are filtered out based on their relevance, removing
those that are weakly relevant or directly irrelevant. This idea may
sound appropriate, but as demonstrated in [19], the relevance of a
feature does not imply that it belongs or does not to the optimal subset
of features. This concept is known as interaction among features [20]. In
this sense, filters usually yield worse results in terms of accuracy with
respect to wrappers. There are many filtering methods in the literature,
of which Relief [21] and mRMR [22] can be mentioned. Nonetheless,

1.2.2
Wrapper methods
In contrast to filters, wrapper approaches can be understood as proce-
dures consisting of a strategy that guides the search through iterations,
while an induction algorithm evaluates each potential solution. How-
ever, wrappers suffer from the high execution time required to obtain
the final subset of features that best represents the original dataset.
With this in mind, it becomes crucial to apply different strategies to
improve their efficiency. The procedures developed in this dissertation
belong to wrapper approaches.
1.2.2.1
Search strategy
The first issue that must be tackled when developing a wrapper is the
strategy to guide the search process. In the first place, the proposed
methods to carry out the search process were divided into two groups:
constructive models and local search models. The former start from
an arbitrary solution and add components until they obtain the final
solution. These models have the drawback that they usually get stuck
at local optima, leading to rather poor solutions. In this context, local
search models obtain better solutions, as long as there is a balance
between intensification and diversification to identify relevant regions
of the search space and not waste time in those that are not. Many local
search models have been proposed over the years, such as SA [23, 24],
SA: Simulated
Annealing
TS [25], VNS [26, 27], PSO [28, 29], EAs [30, 31], ACO [32], etc. Their
TS: Tabu Search
VNS: Variable
Neighborhood
Search
PSO: Particle
Swarm Optimization
ACO: Ant Colony
Optimization
main difference lies in the number of solutions they use in the search
process. Thus, they can be classified into two types:
1. Trajectory models. They start from a single initial solution and
create a "trajectory" in the search space until they reach the final
solution. In general, at each iteration, the closest neighbors are
analyzed to find a better solution, although sometimes a worse
solution may be chosen to promote diversification in the search
and provide a mechanism for escaping from local optima. This
first group includes models such as SA or TS.
2. Population-based models. They address a defined set (i.e., a pop-
ulation) of solutions, which can either evolve independently or


1.3 evolutionary algorithms
13
form new solutions by recombining with each other. Initially
involving a single population, they have evolved into multi-
population approaches. Given their nature, these models provide
a greater diversification in the search with respect to trajectory
models, although the intensification is also contemplated through
various techniques of each algorithm. This second group includes
models such as PSO, ACO, or EAs.
1.2.2.2
Induction algorithm
It is essential to evaluate each potential wrapper solution to direct the
search process. The induction algorithm, which fulfills this function,
must be selected based on the specific problem at hand, since not all FS
problems have the same nature. Depending on the data, FS problems
can be classified into two types: supervised (classification or regression)
[33] and unsupervised (clustering) [34]. First, classification algorithms
are used when dealing with problems with discrete outputs, commonly
called labels [33, 35, 36]. Secondly, regression algorithms are those
whose outputs are continuous, giving rise to numeric values. Finally,
in clustering algorithms, no output is available since their purpose is
to split the data into different clusters. Since the type of data used in
this thesis has a discrete output in the form of labels, the induction
algorithm used is framed within the supervised classification.
1.3
evolutionary algorithms
One of the most commonly used search strategies in wrapper ap-
proaches, and the ones that have enjoyed the greatest recognition
by the scientific community, are EAs, which can be understood as a
population-based stochastic procedure inspired by Charles Darwin’s
theory of natural evolution [37, 38]. There are many types of EAs such
as EP [39], ESs [40], GAs [30, 31], and GP [41], although they differ only

Programming
ES: Evolutionary
Strategies
GA: Genetic
Algorithms
GP: Genetic
Programming
in the way they represent the individuals of the population. Basically,
the main goal of this type of algorithm is to solve combinatorial (NP-
NP: Non-
deterministic
Polynomial-time
hard) problems in which the best solution, known as global optimum,
or optima in multimodal problems, is unknown a priori. Problems
characterized by the curse of dimensionality belong to this type. Because
obtaining this solution is infeasible in polynomial time, EAs are reliable
enough to achieve solutions very close to this desired solution. This
process is known as convergence and is achieved as long as the EA is
properly designed.

Figure 1.2: EA’s main steps.
Figure 1.2 illustrates the main phases of an EA. First, individuals are
initialized based on the representation that best suits the problem to be
solved. Next, a selection mechanism is conducted to choose the parents
that will produce offspring through the recombination process, which
is formed by crossover and mutation. Then, offspring is evaluated by
the objective function so that each individual has a quality assessment
known as fitness. Finally, the selection process is in charge of choosing
the individuals that will form the population for the next generation,
with the fittest individuals being more likely to survive. This process is
repeated iteratively until convergence, or any other stop criterion, is
satisfied.
1.3.1
Fitness function
As mentioned throughout this section, the fitness or objective function
is responsible for providing individuals with a measure of quality,
which is the key to guide the search in successive generations. This
fitness function may consist of one objective (single-objective), a few
objectives, 2 or 3, (multi-objective), or many objectives, 4+, (many-
objective). Furthermore, each of them may be minimized or maximized,
depending on the needs of the problem to be addressed. Two very com-
mon objectives for FS problems are the maximization of the classifier
performance and the minimization of the number of selected features.


1.3 evolutionary algorithms
15
1.3.2
Individual representation
The representation of the individuals in the population is the way in
which possible solutions to a real problem are encoded so that an EA
can evolve them. In the world of EAs, the representation of a solution
for a real problem is known as a phenotype, while its encoding within
the EA, is called genotype or chromosome. From now on, in order to
improve reading comprehension in the thesis, each candidate solution
to the problem to be solved is referred to as an individual since this is
the most widely used term by the EA community.
There are various forms of representation [42], the most common
being binary, integer, trees, and real value vectors. It is important to
emphasize that the chosen individual representation determines the
design requirements for crossover and mutation operators. Hence,
before starting the design of any EA, it becomes crucial to decide which
type of representation is chosen.
1.3.3
Generation of the initial population
On the one hand, determining the correct population size for an EA
has become a recurrent issue since this kind of algorithm was born
[43–45]. There is no consensus on the best way to carry out this task
to date. Many times, different population sizes are analyzed before
performing the final experiment. Other times, the problem to be solved
is studied and, based on this, it is decided what population size to use.
On the other hand, it is necessary to define how individuals of the
initial population are generated, since the subsequent search process
depends to a large extent on this issue. Basically, this generation should
to be carried out without any bias and in a random way.
1.3.4
Parent selection mechanism
This is the first step in each iteration or generation of EAs [46], in
which the parents that will create the successive offspring are chosen.
There are many types of selection mechanisms, but most of them
consider the individual’s fitness for the selection of the parents. Here,
individuals with higher fitness have a higher probability of being


16
1 introduction
selected, although individuals with lower fitness may also be selected,
but with a lower probability. However, it should be noted that there are
other mechanisms that select individuals entirely at random, advocating
greater diversification in the search.
1.3.5
Breeding operators
The breeding phase is known to be one of the most relevant in EAs,
since the generation of new individuals (offspring) is conducted here.
This phase, in turn, is subdivided into two steps: crossover and mu-
tation. The former is responsible for the creation of offspring from
the recombination of the parents. By contrast, in the latter, the new
individuals are slightly modified.
1.3.5.1
Crossover
Crossover is a stochastic process in which two parents are combined to
create two offspring. It is called stochastic because the different parts of
the individual, as well as its distribution for each descendant, are chosen
randomly. The purpose of this operator is to create individuals that can
somehow improve the parents through recombination. As occurs in
nature, not all the offspring improve their parents, but some do, thus
ensuring that, along generations, the population evolves properly.
1.3.5.2
Mutation
Like crossover, the mutation process is also considered stochastic. Its
theoretical background lies in the mutation present in nature whereby,
any gene can randomly undergo a variation, giving rise to individu-
als with different features. This variation could cause either the new
individual to worsen or to improve the previous one. In the context of
EAs, the purpose of mutation is both to promote diversification in the
search and to provide a mechanism to escape from local optima.
1.3.5.3
Application probabilities
Both crossover and mutation have two associated probabilities of ap-
plication, pc and pm, respectively. Typically, pc is set at a high value to


1.3 evolutionary algorithms
17
produce a sufficient number of offspring. Conversely, it must be kept
in mind that the value for pm should be low, otherwise a blind search
would be conducted.
1.3.6
Survivor selection mechanism
The term survivor selection, environmental selection, or replacement is a
process, similar to parent selection described above in Section 1.3.4,
by which the individuals that conform the population for the next
generation are selected based on their fitness, with the fittest ones
being more likely to be chosen. Although any selection process within
an EA is stochastic, selection pressure can be increased through elitism
[47], as NSGA-II [48] does, for example.
NSGA: Non-
dominated Sorting
Genetic Algorithm
There are different heuristics for choosing the population that passes
to the next generation. One possibility is to choose individuals directly
from the offspring, discarding the parent population. Alternatively,
both populations could participate in the selection of new individuals.
In general, the size of the final population is usually the same as that
of the original one, but it could also be different.
1.3.7
Stop criterion
The purpose of any EA is to evolve the population until convergence is
reached. Nonetheless, this convergence is not the same for all cases, so
it should be defined according to the problem to be solved. It has been
theoretically shown that EAs converge in infinite time but, as can be
intuited, this is unfeasible at a practical level. Thus, a stop criterion can
be established, such as those based on the population quality [49–51].
Though, it may happen that the established criterion is never fulfilled.
In this case, it is necessary to define additional criteria to stop the
algorithm if convergence is not reached. Among the most common are
those based on the number of evaluations or generations performed.
Adequately defining these strategies ensures that the algorithm achieves
appropriate results.

1.4
efficient computing
As discussed throughout this chapter, wrapper procedures are char-
acterized by being computationally very demanding, since each of
the possible solutions must be evaluated throughout iterations. It is
therefore important to provide efficient computation mechanisms and
strategies in order to speed up processing and save resources. In this
sense, it is essential to take advantage of the computational capabilities
of current computers.
Computers have evolved throughout history from simple, but huge,
machines capable of solving arithmetic operations to the ones available
today, whose computing power has increased exponentially, being able
to solve a multitude of tasks of many kinds. However, during the last
decades, an environmentally sustainable technological development
is becoming more and more relevant. In a globalized world of limited
resources and an increasing demand for energy [52], it is crucial to
analyze whether it is possible to carry out the same task by decreasing
its execution time while consuming less energy [53, 54]. One of the
main reasons for this trend is that the end of Moore’s law is in sight [55].
The technological evolution lies mainly in the reduction of lithography
in the manufacture of integrated circuits, which is gradually reaching
its physical limit, causing this reduction to become more and more
challenging [56, 57]. Thus, new strategies of parallel programming,
efficient code development, HPC systems, etc., become essential for the

Performance
Computing
execution of heavy tasks in bioinformatics.
1.4.1
Preliminary concepts
Before getting into all the issues related to the development of an
efficient code, it is necessary to know some basic concepts to achieve a
better understanding. Specifically, these concepts are:
• Process. It is the instance of a computer program that is scheduled
on the CPU for execution. A process is more than the program
code, as it includes the process stack, program counter, registers,
virtual address space, a security context, etc. This process-related
information is called context. In addition, the main characteristic
of a process is that it is a single unit with its own allocated mem-
ory region. Therefore, tasks such as inter-process communication,
context switching, or process creation and destruction are compu-
tationally cumbersome. Finally, a process can also create several


1.4 efficient computing
19
children processes, which have their own execution context and
memory region.
• Thread. It is a segment or a subpart of a process, which means
that a process can have multiple threads associated with it. The
main difference with processes is that all threads share the same
memory region of their parent process, so any operation (creation,
destruction, communication, etc.) is much more efficient than in
the case of multiple independent processes.
• Task. The term task is not without ambiguity, as it can be consid-
ered synonymous with process or thread in certain OSs. However,
OS: Operating
System
in the majority of contexts, a task can be defined as a discrete unit
of execution or work, that is, any operation assigned by the OS
for execution.
• Communication. The way of exchanging information between
different tasks is called communication. This in turn can be syn-
chronous or asynchronous. In the former, the communication is
not finished until the receiving task gets the information from
the sending task and both are synchronized. On the contrary,
in an asynchronous communication, the sending side sends the
message and does not wait until the receiving side gets it, so it
can continue its execution flow.
• Heterogeneity/Homogeneity. Although these concepts do not
apply only to computing, it may be useful to recall their meaning.
On the one hand, a computer system is homogeneous when each
of its parts has the same characteristics. On the other hand, a
system is considered heterogeneous when at least one of its parts
has different characteristics from the rest. Heterogeneity and ho-
mogeneity are commonly used in high-performance clusters, in
which each node can have the same or different specifications.
In each case, the code should be developed considering these
characteristics to achieve maximum leverage of the cluster com-
putational resources.
• Memory access. There are typically two main approaches: UMA
UMA: Uniform
Memory Access
and NUMA. Basically, the main difference between them lies in
NUMA: Non-
Uniform Memory
Access
how memory access is managed. In UMA approaches, memory
access is uniform for each processor, with constant access time
and latency, since there is a single memory controller. On the
contrary, in NUMA approaches, each processor has its own con-
troller so the access time depends on how close the memory is to
the processor.

1.4.2
Code optimization
When creating code, it is necessary to take into consideration all the
techniques that allow the code to be as optimal as possible. This opti-
mization, contrary to what many programmers think, should be carried
out during the coding process, not at the end. However, first, it should
be clarified what optimizing is. This concept is very abstract and, de-
pending on the context, can have different meanings. In embedded
systems, an optimal code may be the one that occupies the least amount
of memory because these devices generally have restrictions on the
available resources. Conversely, in many applications, an optimal code
is one that can reduce execution time, energy consumption, or both
while maintaining its functionality. Over the years, compilers have pro-
vided tools to optimize code automatically. Though, no optimization
is as efficient as the one performed by any programmer with good
coding habits. In either case, optimizations are divided into two types:
architecture-independent and architecture-dependent.
On the one hand, architecture-independent optimizations are those that
are independent of the machine in which the code is executed. A
typical example would be to use algorithms with a lower complexity
order. Loop unrolling is another widely used technique since loops
are usually the most computationally intensive parts of a program. It
is common for some loops to perform a single arithmetic operation
(addition, subtraction, multiplication, etc.), so loop unrolling is based on
performing this operation several times in the same iteration, instead
of just once. Therefore, a reduction in loop management instructions
(increase of pointers, decrease in counters, etc.) helps improve efficiency.
Finally, the optimization called dead code elimination can be mentioned,
which eliminates the code that has no impact on the final execution
(variables that are never used, function calls that are never performed,
memory reservation that is never allocated, etc.).
On the other hand, architecture-dependent optimizations are those that
rely on the architecture of the machine in which the code is executed.
Thus, the binary file generated or the script created only works correctly
on that machine. This type of optimizations are usually more efficient
than those mentioned in the previous paragraph because the device
characteristics are considered. However, their main disadvantage is the
limitation of portability, since the code can only be executed on the
machine for which it was designed. A wide number of optimizations
can be listed here [58–60], but one of the most relevant is vectorization
following the SIMD scheme [61–63], in which CPU registers are used

1.4.3
Parallel programming
The first two concepts to consider when working with parallel codes to
be run in one single computer are those that define the way tasks are
distributed: multiprocessing and multithreading. In the former, as many
processes as desired are created, each one having its own independent
memory area. This type of parallelism is not the most efficient since,
the greater the number of processes created, the greater the amount of


22
1 introduction
memory used. In addition, communication between different processes
is more costly as they do not share the same memory region. On
the contrary, thread-based parallelism is a radically opposite concept.
Here, there is only one parent, or master, process in charge of creating
the rest of the threads, which share the same memory region (shared
memory) of the master process, so the amount of memory used is
considerably less than in multiprocessing. Moreover, in multithreading,
communication between threads is very efficient, since they all access
the same region of memory. In this sense, thread-based parallelism is
always preferable to process-based parallelism, whenever possible.
In light of the aforementioned considerations, it is possible to com-
prehend parallelism at two distinct levels [64, 65]. The first of these
is task parallelism, which involves the decomposition of the problem
into multiple subtasks that are executed in parallel. Three of the most
relevant approaches to task parallelism are:
• Fork/Join. This is one of the most widely used schemes. At the
beginning of the program, there is only a single task that is
executing the program sequentially. When the parallel region or
zone is reached, different tasks are created, executing in parallel.
At the end of this region, all the chidren tasks are destroyed and
converge to the main one, which continues the program flow
sequentially.
• Master/Worker. Here, a master or manager distributes the tasks
to be executed to the different workers, which compute in par-
allel. Communication is only between master and worker, never
between workers. On the one hand, the function of the master is
to balance the load so that there is no idle worker waiting for a
task. On the other hand, workers are only limited to computing
and requesting tasks from the master.
• Islands. In this scheme, the different tasks are created at the
beginning of the program execution and are not destroyed until
its completion. Communication, which can be synchronous or
asynchronous, is optional since a scenario in which each island
computes its task independently (isolated islands) and never
communicates with the rest can be adopted [66]. However, this
communication usually takes place to a lesser or greater extent.
Each task, in turn, can perform data parallelism, depending on the
problem to be addressed, if dedicated hardware is available. Basically,
this type of parallelism concerns performing the same operation on

several different pieces of data in parallel. The vectorization technique
outlined in Section 1.4.2 is an illustration of data parallelism.
1.5
conclusions
This initial chapter has provided an overview of the fundamental
concepts that are further explored in subsequent chapters of this disser-
tation. First, the thesis has been placed within the ML pipeline, a series
of steps that allow computers to identify patterns in vast amounts
of data and make predictions about unknown samples. Specifically,
the fourth phase, concerning FS, is the framework in which the pro-
posed procedures are developed. At this stage, the data are already
pre-processed, normalized, and free of outliers, but with a very high
number of features. This can distort the model to be created, so it is
necessary to apply techniques to identify the most relevant features,
eliminating those that are redundant or irrelevant.
Historically, the two most prevalent approaches for FS problems have
been filters and wrappers. The former select features based on statistical
tests, so they are less computationally demanding. By contrast, wrap-
per approaches comprise a search strategy along with an induction
algorithm, classification in this case. While wrappers require significant
computational resources, they are capable of identifying solutions that
frequently outperform those generated by filters, since the induction
algorithm is used within the search process. In this sense, EAs, which
encode potential solutions as individuals that evolve over generations,
can be considered a highly relevant search engine. During the process,
individuals are crossed to obtain higher quality offspring, while at the
same time they may undergo mutations. Finally, the best individuals
survive to form the new population that passes to the next generation.
Having introduced wrappers as a metaheuristic suitable for FS prob-
lems and EAs as a commonly used search strategy, the next chapter
examines the most relevant state-of-the-art on EA-based wrappers,
identifying the different approaches for each of its parts. In addition,
an analysis of which classification algorithms have been mostly used
is presented, with k-NN highlighted as one of the most important

ones. To develop each of these procedures, it is essential to choose
an appropriate programming language. In this regard, the following
chapter focuses on the discussion of Python, which is one of the most
important languages within the ML community.

On the other hand, wrappers have a high computational demand due
to the necessity of evaluating a vast number of potential solutions.
Thus, this chapter has introduced some key concepts related to efficient

Python, the next chapter provides an analysis of the different ways to

Chapter 1 presented the different stages of the ML pipeline, framing
the thesis in its fourth phase, i.e., FS. It also addressed the two ap-
proaches most commonly used for FS (wrappers and filters), detailing
the main features of each. Wrappers usually achieve superior results
compared to filters, since they search for the best subset of features
along with an induction algorithm (classification in this case) that eval-
uates each possible solution to the problem. In this sense, wrappers are
an adequate option to address high-dimensional FS problems.
One area for examination within the context of wrapper approaches
is the search strategy. In the previous chapter, EAs were identified
as a reliable solution, so EA-based wrappers are analyzed in-depth
in Section 2.1. This includes the most appropriate objective function
for FS problems, the type of representation used, which conditions
the breeding operators, the stop criterion of the algorithm, the parent
selection mechanism, and the generation of the initial population. As
discussed in Section 2.1.1, FS problems are commonly addressed as
MOOPs, which has prompted some implementation changes in EAs
MOOP: Multi-
Objective
Optimization
Problem
compared to those outlined in Section 1.3, such as the introduction
of a dominance criterion to be able to compare solutions according
to several conflicting objectives to be optimized simultaneously, and
the fact that there are multiple optimal solutions to a problem with
different trade-offs for the objectives (Section 2.1.2).
It is also important to consider the population structure within EAs.
It has evolved over time from a single-population model to a multi-
population model in which each subpopulation evolves independently,
exchanging individuals only during the migration process. This change
has made multi-population wrappers highly parallelizable, as discussed
in Section 2.2.2. It is essential to ensure that the migration process is
correctly adjusted for a multi-population model to work optimally. This
process, along with the hyperparameters that regulate it, are subjected
to detailed analysis in Section 2.2.1. Furthermore, the classical recom-
mendations for adjusting these hyperparameters and their suitability
in the context of high-dimensional FS problems are also addressed.

Once the search strategy (EA) of the wrapper has been analyzed, the
classification method that evaluates each of the possible solutions
should be discussed. In this sense, k-NN is presented in Section 2.3 as
one of the most widely used classification methods within wrappers
procedures. A detailed overview on how to adjust the method, its
available optimizations, and how both issues influence the performance

Another important consideration when developing an EA-based wrap-

Despite the proven merits of evolutionary wrappers for addressing
high-dimensional FS problems, their main drawback is the high com-
putational cost involved. This could be mitigated by a parallel multi-
population model, as previously discussed. However, it is unclear how
this implementation would affect energy consumption, as more CPU
cores would be in use compared to a sequential version. In addition,
the different hyperparameters of the migration process could influence
both the effectiveness and the efficiency of the procedure. Thus, it is es-
sential to assess the impact of each implementation and parametrization
on resource consumption in order to identify the most energy-aware
solution. In this sense, Section 2.5 discusses the use of smart meters for
this purpose.
Finally, many wrapper designs and parameterizations must be analyzed
to identify the best one for high-dimensional FS problems. In addition,
its results must also be compared with those of other state-of-the-art
wrappers in order to obtain a competitive solution. Since an EA-based
wrapper is to be developed, its results can be seen as samples from
unknown distributions for several metrics, such as its solutions quality,
its computation time or its consumed energy. Therefore, the application
of statistical tests to analyze and compare these results distributions

2.1.1
Fitness function for FS problems
The first issue to address when approaching any optimization prob-
lem is to define the fitness function, since this function is responsible
for guiding the search toward optimal solutions, as discussed in Sec-
tion 1.3.1. It is clear that FS problems require a significant reduction
in the number of features to eliminate any that may distort the final
model. However, this process must not compromise the efficacy of the
model, as this would render it useless. Conversely, maximizing this ef-
fectiveness without considering the reduction of dimensionality would
be counterproductive, as it could result in overfitting (Section 1.1.6),
as well as failing to implement any FS process. Thus, it is essential to
achieve a balance between these two a priori conflicting objectives [97,
98], since the purpose of any wrapper lies precisely there: to achieve
the subset of features that best represents the original dataset with the
lowest possible complexity. This type of optimization problem, in which
two or three objectives are optimized, is known as MOOP. However,
there are some FS procedures that use a single-objective optimization
approach, such as [91], but they cannot be considered pure SOOPs
SOOP: Single-
Objective
Optimization
Problem
because they optimize one objective without compromising the other,
so they are really MOOPs.
With this in mind, the two objectives commonly optimized in the
majority of multi-objective wrapper procedures for FS problems are:
the maximization the classifier accuracy, or reducing the classification


30

error, and the reduction of the number of selected features. Determining
the number of selected features is immediate and no specific metric is
needed. Nonetheless, measuring the efficacy of a classifier is not trivial,
and many metrics, such as accuracy, recall, F1-score, false positive rate,
false negative rate, or classification error, have been proposed. One of
the most robust measures is the Kappa index [99] since in addition to
evaluating the accuracy of the classifier, it also considers the per-class
error distribution.
2.1.2
Multi-objective optimization
Since the solutions in SOOPs are completely ordered, the search al-
gorithm is designed to return a single solution, the best one found.
However, MOOP’s objectives are conflicting, leading to a partially or-
dered set of solutions. This means that there are different solutions
that are better than the rest but have different satisfaction trade-offs for
each objective. These solutions are called Pareto-optimal solutions [100].
Thus, the goal for MOOPs is to find as many Pareto-optimal solutions
as possible, providing a variety of trade-offs for the objectives. Then,
the DM can choose the solution that better fits his preferences.

Manager
The dominance criterion, outlined below, enables the partial ordering
of solutions and facilitates the identification of the Pareto-optimal
solutions.

2.1.5.1
Binary representation
The crossover operators related to the binary representation are typi-

exchanged between the two parents, resulting in two offspring with a

of the most prevalent. In essence, all the features are considered inde-

crossover operators are illustrated in Figure 2.3. For further insight into

2.1.8
Generation of the initial population
An appropriate initial population is key for an EA to achieve satisfactory
solutions to a problem. Two fundamental aspects come into play: the
population size and the generation of its individuals. The number
of individuals (ni) should be adequate so that the population size
is neither too small nor too large. A small number of individuals
would not adequately cover the search space, thus running the risk
of stagnating in local optima. Conversely, too large a population size
could unnecessarily extend the convergence time without enhancing
the quality of the solutions found with a population correctly sized,
resulting in an increased consumption of computational resources.
Although some studies set ni to a fixed value without any particular
heuristic [123–126], it is not advisable to adjust the number of individ-
uals without considering the problem addressed, as this is likely to
result in an inappropriate population size that runs the aforementioned
risks. A suitable population size can always be found by trying several
values and choosing the one that gives the best results, as discussed
in Section 1.3.3. However, this approach would lead to a significant
increase in resource consumption. Fortunately, works such as [51, 90,
127] have proposed to set the population size to a value close to the
number of features in the dataset, i.e., ni ≈n f , in order to cover the
search space more accurately.
Regardless of the population size chosen, individuals should be gen-
erated without any bias, as there is no point in having a population
of adequate size if the features initially selected by the individuals
are biased or not stochastically distributed over the search space. In
this sense, a widely accepted approach is to select each feature with
a probability of p f = 0.5 when generating an individual for the initial
population [128–130]. However, this heuristic produces initial individu-
als with an average size of n f /2, which can be a very high number of
selected features for high-dimensional FS problems compared to the
final subsets obtained after the wrapper has converged. In this sense,
it would be interesting to study whether it is possible to decrease this
probability without affecting the quality of the final solutions to reduce
the number of generations needed to achieve convergence.

2.1.9
Parent selection mechanism
As outlined in Section 1.3.4, the parent selection mechanism is respon-
sible for choosing the individuals which will produce the subsequent
offspring. While there are numerous mechanisms for fulfilling this
function [46], two of the most prevalent are the roulette and the tourna-
ment mechanisms. The former behaves much like a standard roulette
wheel in a casino, but with an individual’s probability of selection
directly proportional to its fitness. This ensures that the most qualified
individuals are more likely to be selected as parents. However, this
mechanism is highly susceptible to stochastic noise. Furthermore, it is
a more costly solution than the tournament selection [131, 132], which
can be described as follows. For the selection of each parent, two indi-
viduals are randomly selected and the best one is chosen as the parent.
For SOOPs, this choice is immediate, but for MOOPs, the dominance
criterion (2.1) should be applied. First, if one individual dominates the
other, the dominant individual is chosen. On the contrary, one of the
two is chosen randomly.
2.1.10

Given that high-dimensional datasets often have a limited number of
samples, it is crucial for the wrapper method to have a mechanism in
place to avoid overfitting. Usually cross-validation [19, 133] is used to
address this issue. Nevertheless, applying cross-validation to evaluate
all the solutions in the population in all the generations of a MOEA

2.1.11
Stop criterion
Due to the non-deterministic behavior of EAs, it is necessary to define
a stop criterion to terminate the search. Briefly, stop criteria can be di-
vided into two types: local (iteration-wise) and global (execution-wise).
For the former, only solutions belonging to the current iteration are
compared with a desired solution. The main disadvantage of this type
of stopping criteria is that it requires prior knowledge of the problem,
so it is hardly applicable to FS problems, whose global optimum is
unknown. By contrast, a global stopping criterion examines the solu-
tions obtained by the algorithm throughout the iterations and analyzes
when it has converged because no better solutions are obtained.
Nonetheless, many studies have chosen to specify a fixed number of
iterations or generations, but this type of heuristic is not always the
most appropriate because the number of generations needed to find
satisfactory solutions is unknown a priori. The algorithm may stop be-
fore convergence, or on the contrary, it may run more generations than
necessary, increasing both execution time and energy consumption.
Thus, establishing a stopping criterion based on the number of itera-
tions would be interesting as a complement to another type of stopping
criterion, i.e., convergence detection. If the latter is not met, the search
could be stopped after a predetermined number of generations so the
search does not extend indefinitely.
Many different ways of stopping an EA have been suggested over the
years, including studies such as [49, 134–136]. However, criteria based
on the estimation of the population quality have been used in many
successful studies. These criteria can be framed within the global type
because the desired solution is unknown. Also, the evolution of these
measures is analyzed over time and within a single generation.
2.2
multi-population approaches
Population-based models have enjoyed considerable popularity since
their inception [137–142] because they can achieve a good balance
between intensification and diversification. Although initially these
procedures involved a single population of individuals, they evolved
into multi-population models through the years. The first author to
officially propose a multi-population model was Wilson in 1967 [143],
and since then, they have been used in countless problems. It should


44
2 related work
be noted that these models are also referred to as island-based models
in many studies.
In essence, a multi-population model comprises a number of subpopu-
lations that evolve independently, exchanging individuals at regular
intervals. One of the most common approaches to establishing each
subpopulation is to distribute the individuals from the original popula-
tion into the different subpopulations, as R. Tanese outlined in [144].
This way of distributing the individuals allows to broad the search
space spectrum and makes them highly parallelizable. Because of this,
problems with larger populations can be addressed more plausibly, as
the individuals that make up such a population can be divided into
subpopulations that evolve independently, for example, on different
CPU cores or even different computers.
2.2.1
Migration process
One of the keys in multi-population models is the migration process,
which is defined as the movement of individuals between subpopula-
tions every certain number of generations. This exchange of individuals
may favor the injection of higher quality solutions into subpopulations
potentially stuck in local optima, thus promoting diversity in the search
space. With this in mind, this section outlines issues such as the hyper-
parameters that regulate migration process, historical recommendations
for adjusting them, recent studies that have endeavored to shed light on
the subject of their adjustment, and, finally, an analysis of the suitability
of these recommendations for high-dimensional FS problems.
2.2.1.1
Hyperparameter definition
Specifically, the six hyperparameters that regulate the migration process
are:
• Migration interval (mi). Also known as period in many studies,
it indicates the number of iterations that must elapse between
each migration process. Although it is usually set to a fixed value,
some studies have considered adjusting it dynamically during
the search [145–147].


2.2 multi-population approaches
45
• Migration policy (mp). It defines how migrants are selected from
the source subpopulation and how they are integrated into the
destination one.
• Migration rate (mr). Also known as grain, it indicates the number
of individuals (migrants) each subpopulation sends when the
migration occurs.
• Migration topology (mt). It determines how the different subpop-
ulations are connected.
• Number of subpopulations (nsp). Number of subpopulations run-
ning the procedure.
• Subpopulation size (ssp). Number of individuals for each one of
the subpopulations.
2.2.1.2
Classical recommendations
The first relevant approaches to adjustment of the migration process
can be attributed to Cantú-Paz in the late 1990s [66, 148–152]. These
studies aimed to provide a set of recommendations for correct adjust-
ment of the migration process in multi-population models since, up to
that point, there was a proliferation of papers with expensive exper-
iments, making it difficult to establish certain generalization criteria.
Cantú-Paz showed that an appropriate adjustment of the migration
hyperparameters affected the final solution.
On the one hand, Cantú-Paz stated that a degradation in accuracy
could occur if the different subpopulations comprised a significantly
low number of individuals [151], showing the importance of ssp. The
author also discussed that both nsp and ssp had historically been given
less consideration than other factors, such as the number of migrants
and the migration interval
On the other hand, Cantú-Paz also focused on migration policies [152],
more specifically on random-random and best-worst, with the first term
of this terminology indicating how migrants are selected in the source
subpopulation, while the second one describing how the individuals to
be eliminated in the destination subpopulation are chosen to accom-
modate the new ones. Thus, for the random-random policy, individuals
selected in the source subpopulation and those removed in the destina-
tion subpopulation are randomly selected to provide greater genetic


46
2 related work
diversity. In contrast, for the best-worst policy, the worst individuals
of the destination subpopulation are replaced by the best individuals
in the source. Cantú-Paz concluded that the best-worst policy was the
best option since the selection pressure increased with the consequent
acceleration in algorithm convergence.
However, mi and mr were not studied as thoroughly by Cantú-Paz,
although he stated that 0.1 could be an appropriate value for mr [149].
In this sense, studies such as [145, 153, 154] can be highlighted, although
their results vary considerably. On the one hand, [145, 154] suggest
that mr should be set at a relatively low value (as suggested by Cantú-
Paz in [149]) and mi at a moderate value (10 −30 generations). In
contrast, [153] found that the influence of mi and mr is residual when
the population is large enough, also in agreement with the conclusions
of Cantú-Paz [151].
Subsequently, Tomassini presented one of the most relevant experi-
mental works on migration tuning [155], in which some guidelines for
migration hyperparameters adjustment were established. Here, classi-
cal problems such as the Even-Parity-4 or the Artificial Ant on the Santa
Fe Trail were solved, with populations of 100, 500, or 2 500 individu-
als distributed into up to 50 subpopulations. In summary, the main
conclusions reached were as follows:
• Distributing individuals in isolated subpopulations [66], in which
migration did not occur at any time, provided better results than
using a single population.
• By including the migration process in the isolated subpopulation
scheme, better solutions were achieved, mainly due to the injec-
tion of individuals from other subpopulations, which improved
search diversity.
• The adopted topology was not a fundamental factor, although
the best results were obtained with the Ring topology, resulting
in significant computational savings.
• Finally, a study was tackled to adjust the values of mi and mr
through a combination of different values. In this case, 5 subpop-
ulations with 100 individuals each were used. Basically, it was
concluded that mi should take either 5 or 10, while mr should be
set to 0.1 or 0.15. To a greater or lesser extent, this follows the
trend previously reported in [145, 154].

• Furthermore, despite not being the best option, it could also be
observed that if mi increased, mr should increase accordingly. If
migrations occurred sporadically, more individuals were to be
injected to promote genetic diversity. Conversely, if mi was very
low, causing migrations to happen very frequently, mr should
also be decreased accordingly to prevent the algorithm from
converging prematurely. Otherwise, many individuals would
migrate between subpopulations too quickly, causing all of them
to start sharing the same individuals after only a few generations.
This lack of diversity would negatively affect the quality of the
final solutions, stagnating the algorithm at local optima.
2.2.1.3
Recent studies
Although most studies set their migration processes based on the
guidelines mentioned above, some works have tried to contribute their
grain of sand to this subject. They can be split into two types depending
on the population sizes they use.
On the one hand, works such as [156–158] can be highlighted, in which
some novel metaheuristics are used for small populations. Here, mi,
mr, nsp, and ssp are analyzed, with ssp ranging from 60 to 100 and
nsp from 2 to 15, by evaluating a set of IEEE-CEC2005 unimodal and
multimodal benchmark functions with different complexity. Although
the trend is toward tuning mi to intermediate values and mr to relatively
low values, as Tomassini noted, it seems that the adjustment of the
migration process depends on the metaheuristic and the functions to
be optimized. Anyway, due to the small size of the population and the
type of problem addressed in these studies, these conclusions should
not be extrapolated for large population setups. Of particular interest
for mt is [159], which divides a population of 100 individuals into 1
to 12 subpopulations to determine the relationship between migration
topology and problem structure. Several topologies (including Ring,
Fully connected, Grid, and others) are examined, and it is concluded
that none is inherently the best in all scenarios because the relationship
between the population structure and the problem is highly complex.
Finally, in relation to mp, [160] agrees with the findings of Cantú-Paz
and suggests that the best-worst policy is the most appropriate approach.
On the other hand, concerning medium or large-sized populations, the
work [161] can stand out, in which 2 048 individuals are distributed into
10 subpopulations. Here, the best value for mi is analyzed, concluding
that small intervals should be avoided, although the remaining hyper-

parameters are not studied in depth. However, [162] states that a large
number of individuals should migrate in short migration intervals,
which conflicts with the recommendation of [161]. This could be caused
by the fact that each hyperparameter is studied in isolation, leading
to contradictory conclusions. Concerning mt, Ruci´nski addressed the
study of this hyperparameter for large populations in [163], conclud-

(Ring + 1 + 2 and Ring + 1 + 2 + 3) provided the best results. Finally, in

that best-worst is the most appropriate as it is consistent with the natural
selection mechanism for survival of the fittest.
2.2.1.4
Adjustment suitability for high-dimensional FS problems
Although the recommendations made by Cantú-Paz and Tomassini
for tuning the migration process were made 20 years ago, they con-
tinue to be applied currently in addressing FS problems [81, 85, 86,
165], even though their scale has grown significantly and much larger
populations are needed to maintain the diversity across the search
space [90, 166–169], as discussed in Section 2.1.8. With this in mind, the
following question arises: Are these guidelines still valid today when
the complexity of FS problems and the size of the populations needed
to find adequate solutions have increased considerably? To the best of
our knowledge, this topic remains an open front.
Related to the previous question, an equally relevant one arises: How
does the adjustment of the migration hyperparameters affect the ef-
ficiency of the procedure? Usually, the quality of the final results is
first considered. Nonetheless, both the execution time and the energy
consumption of the proposal should not be neglected. In a world of
limited resources and a climate change of increasing concern, the de-
velopment of energy-efficient approaches is essential [53, 54]. In this
sense, the problem of fitting the migration hyperparameters for the
large populations needed by high-dimensional FS problems should be
tackled to obtain quality solutions, but also caring about the execution
time or the energy consumption through efficient computation.
It should be noted that not all migration hyperparameters have been
given the same level of attention. Most studies have focused on the anal-
ysis of mi, mr, relegating nsp and ssp to a secondary role, which could
be counterproductive, as stated by Cantú-Paz in [151]. However, there

appears to be a consensus in the literature regarding the adjustment of

One the one hand, although other migration policies have been pro-
posed, such as [96, 170, 171], many are based on the best-worst one to a
greater or lesser extent. This reinforces the recommendation put forth
by Cantú-Paz in [152]. Here, he concluded that thanks to this migration
policy the selection pressure was increased with the consequent acceler-

the best-worst migration policy is strongly influenced by the kind of

solutions belonging to the Pareto front are usually found for MOOPs.
Thus, many works have chosen to adapt the best-worst policy to this
kind of problem over the years, proposing the selection of migrants
from the Pareto front. In this sense, works such as [172–177] can be
highlighted, in which several novel implementations are carried out
based on this approach aiming at favoring elitism. Besides, observing
only the Pareto front to select migrants is particularly interesting for
large populations, such as those needed for high-dimensional FS prob-
lems, since it favors selection pressure while reducing the number of
individuals considered.
On the other hand, considering the studies of Tomassini [155] and Ru-
ci´nski [163], it seems that it does not make sense to continue exploring
the mt tuning since the Ring topology or versions based on it have
provided good results in a wide range of problems [178–180]. Moreover,
more complex topologies have not achieved better results despite being
more computationally demanding.
Finally, it is remarkable the absence of an experimental study that
takes into consideration both the number of subpopulations and their
size, along with the rest of the migration hyperparameters, to analyze
different values for each of them and their interaction in the context of
current high-dimensional FS problems.
2.2.2
Parallelization scheme
As mentioned above, multi-population models are highly paralleliz-
able because each subpopulation evolves independently, except for the
migration process that takes place every few generations. Two of the
most commonly used schemes are based on the independent evolu-
tion of each subpopulation on different CPU cores (multi-core) or on
different nodes of a high-performance cluster (distributed systems)


50
2 related work
[181–183]. Processes or threads can be responsible for managing this
procedure, but for practical purposes, both strategies should be equally
efficient in most cases (see Section 1.4.3), since communication between
subpopulations is infrequent (only during migration).
An important aspect in parallel multi-population models is how to
perform the migration. This type of communication can be either syn-
chronous or asynchronous. For the former, all the subpopulations
involved in the migration process must synchronize, so the slowest
subpopulation is the one that determines the efficiency of the algorithm.
For this reason, synchronous communication is rarely used, since all
subpopulations evolve independently. In this sense, most studies opt
for an asynchronous communication [184–186], in which each subpop-
ulation sends its migrants to the destination one without stopping its
execution flow. In this way, the efficiency of the procedure is much
higher.
Parallel multi-population models for high-dimensional FS problems
have been widely used in the literature. For example, the approach
proposed in [187] mitigates the high execution time by porting an EA
to a MapReduce implementation suitable for parallelization on a large
number of commodity hardware units using the open source Hadoop
library. Another relevant study is [188], in which a coarse-grained
parallel GA is used to simultaneously optimize the subset of selected
features and the hyperparameters of the SVM. In [189] it is shown that
using a parallel multi-population model increases both the efficiency
and the quality of the solutions found. With respect to distributed
computing, the work proposed in [185] includes a NSGA-II in a parallel
multi-population model to be run on heterogeneous and large-scale
computing platforms. Although the number of works using this kind
of model is very extensive, other studies such as [178, 184, 186, 190–197]
could be highlighted.
