2.3.2
Adjustment of k
Over the years, there has been considerable debate about how to adjust
k correctly [219, 220]. However, as of today, there is no universal heuris-
tic that allows k to be tuned properly for any scenario, although some
recommendations should be considered:
• It is inadvisable to use very low values of k, as this would render
the model highly susceptible to noise, which could result in
overfitting.
• Similarly, very high values of k are not advisable, as this would
lead to underfitting, whereby the generated model exhibits a high
validation error rate due to its inability to accurately capture the
relationship between input and output variables. In addition, this
would result in a significant increase in both execution time and
energy consumption.
• The avoidance of even numbers serves to reduce the likelihood of
a tie in the selection of classes.
Given these considerations, there have been various approaches pro-
posed in the literature to tune k. Some studies have opted to adjust the
value of k through a grid search [221, 222]. The principal advantage of
this approach is that the most suitable value for the hyperparameter
is chosen empirically. However, this method has the disadvantage of a
high computational time to perform this task. Furthermore, establish-
ing how many values to test in the grid search is a matter determined
by the developer, which introduces a potential bias in selecting these
values. In this context, as evidenced by works such as [133, 223, 224],
a suitable value for k appears to be 5, as effective results have been
achieved on a wide range of problems without compromising the effi-
ciency too much. However, this value is relatively modest, potentially
leading to overfitting. In this context, a heuristic has been proposed in
[225] that recommends setting k to the nearest odd value (to reduce the
number of potential ties) of the square root of the number of samples
(ns). Although this heuristic has been shown to work adequately in
studies such as [90, 127, 169, 226], it typically requires more computa-
tional resources than setting k = 5, particularly for high-dimensional
FS problems.


54

2.3.3
k-NN optimizations
The primary disadvantage of the original k-NN method, also called
brute-force k-NN, is the high computational time required as the dataset
size increases, which is determined by the number of samples and the
number of features. Since in the original k-NN each sample to be
classified has to be compared with all training samples, the efficiency
of the method is very susceptible to variations in the dimensionality
and the number of samples of the dataset. To overcome these limitations
in terms of computational efficiency, several implementations of k-NN
using tree-based data structures have been developed.
One of the most relevant approach to be named is the KD-tree k-NN
algorithm [227], which is based on constructing trees to enhance the ef-
ficiency of accessing different samples, thus circumventing the distance
calculation from the current sample to the rest. This algorithm aims
to significantly improve efficiency as the number of samples increases.
However, many datasets analyzed in FS problems consist of a small
number of samples, because the process of extracting these samples is
a costly process. Under these circumstances, this k-NN version would
experience significant efficiency degradation. Furthermore, as outlined
in [228], although KD-tree k-NN is highly efficient for low-dimensional
datasets (n f < 20), its efficiency worsens as n f increases. Consequently,
this version of k-NN is not a viable solution for high-dimensional FS
problems, such as those addressed in this thesis.
In response to the inefficiency of KD-tree k-NN as the dimensionality of
the dataset grows, Ball tree k-NN [229] was proposed, which constructs
spheres to hold a subset of points, thereby alleviating the computational
burden. However, the primary challenge with this version of k-NN is
the construction of the spheres prior to the execution of the algorithm
for high-dimensional datasets. Since new sphere structures must be
created for the evaluation of each individual in an EA-based wrapper
procedure, the derived overhead is unaffordable.
Additionally, both the KD-tree and the Ball tree k-NN implementations
present issues to be vectorized because the access to both trees and
balls is not coalescent. For this reason, in addition to those mentioned
above, the use of brute-force k-NN is recommended when n f > 15
[228].

appear that a reduction of a program’s execution time is always synony-

2.6
comparison of the evolutionary wrapper results
As previously discussed in this dissertation, EAs are defined by their
stochastic nature, since probabilities are present in key aspects such
as the application of crossover or mutation operators, or the selection
of parents to create offspring. It is clear that EA-based wrappers also
exhibit random behavior. It is therefore imperative to apply statistical
analysis to the results provided by the wrapper to ensure a fair and
accurate comparison between them and those obtained by other wrap-
pers, or when different designs or parameterizations of the developed
wrapper are analyzed. This is why this type of wrapper is often exe-
cuted multiple times under the same experimental conditions to obtain
a sampling of its results. Specifically, according to [258], the number
of repetitions should be in the range [20, 50], regardless of the study
addressed.
Although most studies originally compared their results with those of
other approaches using the average of multiple runs, this methodology
was considered unfair, so works such as [259–261] proposed a compari-
son using various parametric tests (ANOVA, t-test, etc.) based on mean
and variance. These tests provide a high level of statistical rigor when
comparing different results sample distributions, although their use is
quite restrictive. Specifically, all results sample distributions must sat-
isfy three conditions: independence, normality, and homoscedasticity.
The most commonly used statistical tests to assess normality are the
Shapiro-Wilk and the Kolmogorov-Smirnov tests. The former is rec-
ommended when the number of samples is less than 50, while the
Kolmogorov-Smirnov test is indicated otherwise. Once normality has
been confirmed, homoscedasticity can be confirmed using the Barlett
test [262, 263].
On the other hand, since the sample distributions of the results may
be neither normal nor homoscedastic, it is particularly interesting to
use non-parametric tests [264], which analyze the median of the results


2.7 conclusions
61
instead of their mean and variance. Among non-parametric tests, the
Kruskal-Wallis test is one of the most relevant methods [265].
In either case, both parametric and non-parametric tests yield a p-value,
which, if less than a certain significance level α, indicates rejection of
the null hypothesis, i.e., that the compared results present statistically
significant differences with a confidence level of (1 −α) × 100%. For
example, rejecting the null hypothesis with a p-value less than α = 0.05
means that the results are different at a confidence level of 95%.
Although a p-value less than α reveals a statistically significant dif-
ference among several results distributions, it does not indicate the
magnitude of that difference. Therefore, only a part of the statistical
study is carried out, as detailed in [266–268]. In this context, a measure
or index called effect size arises, which can be considered equal to
or even more relevant than the p-value. The effect size can be used
to quantify the difference between two result distributions once the
p-value reveals that such a difference exists. Although the effect size
could be considered to have been introduced more than 100 years ago
[269], it was not until the late 1960s that J. Cohen standardized it with
his well-known Cohen’s d index [270].
The study of effect size has gained special relevance in countless stud-
ies, mainly due to the valuable information it provides. This fact is
exemplified in [269], in which it is mentioned that 19 scientific journals
of different natures require a study of the effect size to publish papers.
Over the years, dozens of indexes have been proposed to quantify the
effect size [271, 272], among which Hedge’s g, Pearson’s r, or Glass’s
∆stand out. However, to date, Cohen’s d, which standardizes such a
practical difference or effect size as small (d = 0.2), medium (d = 0.5),
large (d = 0.8), and very large (d ≥1.3), remains one of the most widely
used.
2.7
conclusions
This chapter has provided a comprehensive analysis of all aspects
related to evolutionary wrappers. Firstly, the potential design options
have been explored, highlighting the importance of the fitness function
since is responsible for guiding the search. It has been determined
that a multi-objective optimization is the most suitable approach for
FS problems, in which the accuracy is maximized and the number
of selected features is minimized. Basically, the aim of this type of


62
2 related work
optimization is to identify the greatest number of non-dominated
solutions, also known as the Pareto front.
Among the EAs used for MOOPs, NSGA-II has been identified as
a suitable algorithm. Although it enjoys great popularity because of
its effectiveness, it still presents an important bottleneck for high-
dimensional FS problems because, as discussed in Section 2.1.8, it
is common to have populations with ni ≈n f and the algorithmic
complexity of its fast non-dominated sorting method (FNDS) is O(no ·
ni2).
A potential improvement has been identified regarding the generation
of the initial population for high-dimensional FS problems. Typically,
individuals are generated with a selection probability of p f = 0.5, re-
sulting in individuals with an average size of n f /2. This is a relatively
large size compared to the expected number of features finally selected.
In this sense, it would be interesting to study whether it is possible
to reduce the p f value without affecting the quality of the final solu-
tions, in order to reduce the number of generations needed to achieve
convergence.
Multi-population approaches have enabled EAs to use larger popula-
tions, expanding the search space and enabling them to tackle more
challenging problems. Furthermore, these models are highly paralleliz-
able because each subpopulation evolves independently from the rest
except for the migration process, which has been typically adjusted in
accordance with the guidelines set forth by Cantú-Paz and Tomassini
over two decades ago. However, it is not possible to guarantee that
these recommendations remain applicable to high-dimensional FS prob-
lems. Furthermore, it is essential to evaluate the efficiency of wrappers
in terms of both execution time and energy consumption, taking into
account the adjustments made for the migration process. To the best of
our knowledge, all these issues remain an open front.
This chapter has also discussed the most commonly used classification
methods in EA-based wrappers, focusing on k-NN, a method that has
been identified by the ML community as a versatile, accessible, and
well-supported solution. Despite the existence of alternative tree-based
optimizations of the original brute-force k-NN, a thorough analysis of
them has revealed their unsuitability for addressing high-dimensional
FS problems. Consequently, the original version remains the recom-
mended approach in the context of this dissertation.
Python has been highlighted as the preferred option to develop the
wrapper due to its versatility and popularity within the ML community.


2.7 conclusions
63
However, one significant drawback of Python is its efficiency. This issue
can be alleviated considerably by using libraries such as Scikit-learn or
Numpy, which are coded in C internally. Furthermore, the interpreter
of the Python version used in this dissertation is constrained by the
GIL, which does not allow for the concurrent execution of multiple
threads, so a multiprocessing approach must be used. Nonetheless, this
should not pose a problem for a multi-population wrapper, since each
subpopulation evolves independently and communication is limited to
the migration process.
One of the primary objectives of this dissertation is to minimize wrap-
per energy consumption. To this end, it is necessary to analyze the
energy consumption of the different versions and parameterizations of
the wrapper. The Vampire smart meter has been identified as a solution
that enables the energy consumed by the wrapper to be accurately and
efficiently measured.
In the wrapper optimization path, it is first imperative to prove that the
subsets of features found by the wrapper are competitive with respect
to those obtained by other wrappers, and consequently to analyze the
impact of the different parametrizations and implementations devel-
oped to improve its efficiency and effectiveness. Given the stochastic
component of evolutionary wrappers, it is required to use statistical
tests that allow this study to be carried out in a robust and reliable
manner.
Finally, in light of the aforementioned limitations, the following chapter
presents a series of challenges and propose hypotheses for their resolu-
tion. However, to address each of them, it is necessary to consider other
issues analyzed in this chapter, such as the programming language, the
design and parameterization of an evolutionary wrapper, the proper
measurement of energy consumption, and the statistical tests to per-
form a fair comparison of the behavior of different wrapper alternatives.
These issues, along with the aforementioned hypotheses, result in the
creation of general and specific objectives to be met. Thus, an EA-based
wrapper that can effectively and efficiently address high-dimensional
FS problems can be built.

Conclusions . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . 75
This thesis is focused on developing an optimized EA-based wrapper
for high-dimensional FS problems. Therefore, after a thorough ex-
amination of all relevant aspects related to the design and development
of this type of wrapper in Chapter 2, several potential opportunities
for further study have been identified. In this regard, the three primary
challenges addressed in this doctoral thesis are outlined below.
The first challenge concerns the NSGA-II algorithm, which has been
identified as the most appropriate multi-objective algorithm for the
wrapper search engine in Section 2.1.3.1. One of the key advantages
of NSGA-II is its FNDS method, which fully sorts the union of the
current population and its descendants using the crowded-comparison
operator (≺c), ensuring that the best ni individuals are passed on to the
next generation. However, the complexity order of the FNDS method
is O(no · ni2), and since ni ≈n f for FS problems (see Section 2.1.8),
it becomes clear that this procedure remains a significant bottleneck
in the wrapper for high-dimensional FS problems. Therefore, the first
challenge of this thesis is to mitigate this bottleneck.
Another key aspect discussed in Chapter 2, more specifically in Sec-
tion 2.1.8, was the initialization of the individuals that conform the
initial wrapper population, which is regulated by the hyperparame-
ter p f , typically adjusted to 0.5. The use of the same probability to
select or not each feature when generating an individual for the initial
population results in individuals of an average size of n f /2. This size
can be rather large for high-dimensional FS problems, in which the
subsets of features finally found by the wrapper are likely to have a
considerably smaller number of features. As a result, the procedure
requires a significant number of iterations to converge to the optimal
solution. In this sense, the challenge is to reduce the value of p f with-
out compromising the quality of the solutions in order to accelerate


3.1 hypothesis
67
convergence and subsequently decrease the consumption of resources
derived from the execution of the evolutionary wrapper.
Finally, a really interesting field of study related to evolutionary wrap-
pers was found in the adjustment of the migration process for multi-
population wrappers addressing high-dimensional FS problems (see
Section 2.2.1). Briefly, the migration process facilitates the exchange of
individuals between subpopulations to promote diversity and avoid lo-
cal optima. To date, this adjustment has been carried out in accordance
with the guidelines proposed by Cantú-Paz and Tomassini over two
decades ago. However, the scale of the FS problems and the popula-
tion size required to address them accurately (see Section 2.1.8) have
increased significantly. Consequently, evaluating the suitability of these
guidelines for current high-dimensional FS problems represents an
attractive opportunity, with the potential to enhance the understanding
of a multi-population wrapper in terms of its effectiveness and effi-
ciency. To the best of our knowledge, this topic remains an open front
and an exciting challenge to be met.
A series of hypotheses postulating possible solutions to the above
challenges are formulated in Section 3.1. These hypotheses then lead
to several objectives defined in Section 3.2 to address the challenges.
However, not all the objectives are directly related to facing these
challenges. First and foremost, it is crucial to develop a robust evo-
lutionary wrapper that can effectively address high-dimensional FS
problems, laying the foundation for subsequent implementations. To
achieve this, it is essential to select the appropriate search strategy
and classification algorithm, in line with the recommendations set out
in Chapter 2. Furthermore, additional considerations such as data pre-
processing techniques to remove impurities, the programming language,
and statistical tests for comparing the wrapper behavior with different
implementations or parameterizations, which were discussed in the
previous chapter, must also be taken into account. In this regard, both
the tasks associated with the resolution of the challenges, as well as
those required to achieve that end, have been converted into a series of
general objectives (Ox) and their associated specific objectives (Ox.y).
3.1
hypothesis
After identifying the three main challenges to be faced in this disserta-
tion, this section presents the hypotheses to potentially give an answer
to each of them. It is essential to present these hypotheses in a clear and
concise manner, as the objectives outlined in the subsequent section

3 hypotheses and objectives
are contingent upon the hypotheses presented here. By doing so, it is
possible to make significant progress towards the ultimate objective of
this thesis: develop an evolutionary wrapper that can effectively and
efficiently solve FS problems in high-dimensional spaces.
3.1.1
Hypothesis H1: Solution to NSGA-II’s FNDS bottleneck for high-
dimensional FS problems
The NSGA-II’s FNDS method has a complexity order of O(no · ni2),
which can become a bottleneck for high-dimensional FS problems, since
ni is usually set to a value close to n f . A multi-population model could
help alleviate this issue by reducing the algorithmic complexity by a fac-
tor of nsp. This would result in a complexity order of O(no · (ni/nsp)2)
for each subpopulation. Even for a sequential implementation of the
multi-population wrapper this bottleneck would be considerably miti-
gated, since its order of complexity would be:
O(nsp · no(ni/nsp)2) = O(no · n2
i /nsp)
(3.1)
Furthermore, as each subpopulation evolves independently, with the
exception of the migration process, this model can be easily parallelized,
as discussed in Section 2.2.2. Running each subpopulation in parallel
would therefore result in a further reduction in execution time. The
new order of algorithmic complexity of this parallel wrapper would be:
O(no · (ni/nsp)2)
(3.2)
3.1.2
Hypothesis H2: Acceleration of the wrapper convergence through a
decrease in the average size of individuals in the initial population
Given that individuals of the initial population typically select features
with a probability value of p f = 0.5, what produces individuals with
an average size of n f /2, the hypothesis of decreasing the value of p f to
accelerate convergence is proposed. This approach would create smaller
initial individuals, with an average size closer to that of the solutions
the wrapper will find. Therefore, it is expected that less generations
would be required for the wrapper to converge.


3.1 hypothesis
69
3.1.3
Hypothesis H3: Optimization of the migration hyperparameters for
high-dimensional FS problems
The migration process is usually adjusted according to some guidelines
proposed more than 20 years ago. It is necessary to examine whether
these guidelines are still appropriate in the context of today’s high-
dimensional FS problems. As theoretically outlined by Cantú-Paz in
[151], the number of subpopulations and their size is a crucial element
in multi-population models. However, these two hyperparameters have
historically been given less consideration than other factors, such as the
number of migrants and the migration interval. It is therefore expected
that the population partitioning scheme (nsp, ssp), which involves the
distribution of ni individuals into nsp subpopulations of size ssp (see
Section 2.2), is the key aspect in adjusting the migration process.
In light of these considerations, it is important to note that if individuals
are distributed into an increasing number of subpopulations, there
should come a point in which the subpopulation size becomes so small
that the search is likely to fall into local optima. At this point, it is
hypothesized that there exists a minimum subpopulation size (sspmin)
to avoid the issue of premature convergence. However, once all the
subpopulations have been correctly sized to sspmin, the total population,
ni, which encompasses all subpopulations, would exceed n f for a
sufficiently large number of subpopulations:
nsp > n f /sspmin ⇒ssp = sspmin ⇒ni = nsp · sspmin > n f
(3.3)
Since the wrapper is able to find adequate solutions with ni ≈n f , there
is probably no benefit in setting ni ≫n f , as the wrapper is unlikely to
improve the solutions but the computing time and energy consumption
are likely to raise. Therefore, there should be a maximum threshold for
the number of subpopulations (nspmax) that allows the wrapper to find
appropriate solutions while minimizing its computing time and energy
consumption.
Finally, once the optimal partitioning scheme (nspmax, sspmin) has been
identified, the remaining hyperparameters should play a secondary role
in the behavior of the multi-population wrapper, but they should be
studied to determine their influence and adjust them to an appropriate
value.

3.2
objectives
This section defines the general objectives to be considered in this dis-
sertation in order to confirm each of the previously stated hypotheses.
Furthermore, each general objective is broken down into more detailed
specific objectives to facilitate its fulfillment.
3.2.1
Objective O1: Development of a robust base wrapper
Before addressing the various challenges presented in this chapter, it
is crucial to build a robust EA-based wrapper that can adequately
address high-dimensional FS problems. This procedure forms the basis
for developing subsequent procedures, so it is essential to establish a
solid foundation.
3.2.1.1
Objective O1.1: Implementation of the datasets pre-processing meth-
ods
Prior to developing the base wrapper, it is essential to ensure that
the datasets are adequately prepared (see Section 1.1.3) to enable the
wrapper to achieve appropriate results. Therefore, this specific objective
is dedicated to the development of a data pre-processing methodology
that optimizes the quality of the training data.
3.2.1.2
Objective O1.2: Wrapper design and implementation
This specific objective is focused on the development of a wrapper
that uses NSGA-II as the search strategy and k-NN as the classification
method (see Sections 2.1.3.1 and 2.3, respectively). For this purpose,
each component of the EA must be implemented appropriately, con-
sidering the deliberations presented in Section 2.1. Moreover, given
the analysis of the various k-NN implementations conducted in Sec-
tion 2.3.3, it is essential to identify the most effective approach for
addressing high-dimensional FS problems.
On the other hand, the wrapper must be coded in Python, with the
appropriate libraries selected for efficient computation, since, as dis-
cussed in Section 2.4, this programming language is an excellent option


3.2 objectives
71
for ML procedures, a category in which an EA-based wrapper can be
framed.
3.2.1.3
Objective O1.3: Assessment of the wrapper effectiveness
Ultimately, the results yielded by the wrapper should be evaluated
in comparison with those obtained by other state-of-the-art wrapper
methodologies. This assessment should be substantiated by statistical
analyses, as outlined in Section 2.6, in order to ensure the generation of
well-founded conclusions. The low-, medium-, and high-dimensional
datasets described in Appendix B are utilized for this purpose.
3.2.2
Objective O2: Wrapper optimizations
Once the base wrapper has been developed and its results have been
shown to be appropriate, this general objective addresses Hypotheses
H1 (the solution to NSGA-II’s FNDS bottleneck for high-dimensional
FS problems) and H2 (the acceleration of the wrapper convergence
through a decrease in the average size of individuals in the initial
population).
3.2.2.1
Objective O2.1: Development of a novel migration policy for multi-
objective optimization problems
Prior to addressing the development of the multi-population model
in response to Hypothesis H1, it is essential to define an adequate
migration policy, which is a fundamental aspect of this type of model.
As discussed in Section 2.2.1.4, the best-worst policy appears to be the
most appropriate. However, it should be noted that FS is a MOOP.
Therefore, the individuals in the subpopulations are only partially
ordered, with the best being part of their Pareto fronts. In this sense, a
novel migration policy is the aim of this specific objective, which takes
this peculiarity into account.


72
3 hypotheses and objectives
3.2.2.2
Objective O2.2: Development of a sequential multi-population EA-
based wrapper
Once the migration policy has been defined, Hypothesis H1 postulates
the feasibility of developing a multi-population model to alleviate the
bottleneck caused by the NSGA-II’s FNDS method when processing
high-dimensional FS problems. This model should reduce the FNDS’s
order of complexity by a factor of nsp when using nsp subpopulations.
In this regard, this specific objective addresses the development of this
model, initially sequential, with the aim of alleviating this bottleneck.
3.2.2.3
Objective O2.3: Parallelization of the multi-population EA-based
wrapper
The logical next step after developing a multi-population model is to
apply a parallel strategy, since this type of model is highly parallelizable,
as discussed in Section 2.2.2. It is therefore important to define a
scheme that takes advantage of the multicore capabilities of current
processors. This enables efficient computing in terms of both execution
time and energy consumption. The aim is to develop an efficient parallel
procedure in which each core is responsible for the evolution of a single
subpopulation. Furthermore, the migration must be asynchronous,
as this type of synchronization is more efficient, as also described in
Section 2.2.2.
3.2.2.4
Objective O2.4: Boosting the convergence of the EA-based wrapper by
reducing the average size of the individuals in the initial population
Once the multi-population wrapper has been parallelized, this specific
objective focuses on the study of the hyperparameter p f to give an
answer to Hypothesis H2, that is, if lower p f values, which should
result in a reduction in the average size of individuals in the initial
population, would lead to faster convergence without compromising
the quality of the final solutions. If so, the optimal value for p f must
be determined. Furthermore, it would be worthwhile to verify whether
the value of p f is universal across all datasets or, conversely, dependent
on the specific dataset under analysis.


3.2 objectives
73
3.2.3
Objective O3: Analysis of the migration hyperparameters influence on
the wrapper behavior for high-dimensional datasets
In line with Hypothesis H3 (the optimization of the migration hyper-
parameters for high-dimensional FS problems), the aim of this general
objective is to assess the suitability of the guideliness proposed by
Cantú-Paz and Tomassini for adjusting the migration process, given the
significant increase in the complexity of high-dimensional FS problems
and the population size required to address them. This assessment
must be carried out in accordance with the following specific objectives.
3.2.3.1
Objective O3.1: Analysis of the influence of the population partition-
ing scheme
The population partitioning scheme (nsp, ssp) should be the key ele-
ment in the adjustment of the migration process for high-dimensional
FS problems. In this regard, a variety of partitioning schemes must
be considered, along with a comprehensive range of values for the
remaining migration hyperparameters under analysis. This will result
in an experimental study comprising thousands of experiments, which
should enable an accurate assessment of the impact of the population
partitioning scheme on the efficacy of the multi-population wrapper.
Regardless of the remaining migration hyperparameters, as the number
of subpopulations increases, reducing the number of individuals in
each subpopulation, the likelihood of premature convergence should
also increase due to the smaller size of the subpopulations.
3.2.3.2
Objective O3.2: Optimization of the population partitioning scheme
Once it is confirmed that the wrapper is likely to converge prematurely
to local optima as the subpopulation size decreases, it is necessary
to determine a threshold for the subpopulation size, sspmin, so that
population sizes larger than this threshold should skip such local
optima. Then, after sizing all the subpopulations to such a minimum
population size, a maximum number of subpopulations, nspmax, must
be determined to ensure that the wrapper can find suitable solutions
while making the most efficient use of resources. Thus, the optimal
population partitioning scheme would be (nspmax, sspmin).


74
3 hypotheses and objectives
3.2.3.3
Objective O3.3: Analysis of the influence of the remaining of migra-
tion hyperparameters
Once the optimal population partitioning scheme has been identified
(nspmax, sspmin), the remaining migration hyperparameters under analy-
sis must be studied in detail in order to assess their influence on the
behaviour of the multi-population wrapper.
3.2.4
Objective O4: Development of behavioral comparison procedures
To optimize the wrapper procedure developed in this thesis, it is neces-
sary to compare its behavior obtained using different configurations
and implementations. This enables the selection of the best wrapper ver-
sion. As outlined in Section 2.6, these comparisons must be supported
by statistical tests, so this general objective is focused on providing
procedures to allow such comparisons.
3.2.4.1
Objective O4.1: Development of a dominance criterion to assess the
behavior of the wrapper
The behavior of each wrapper configuration or implementation is re-
lated to the objectives it optimizes and also to some other metrics, such
as its execution time or the energy it consumes. Since several behavioral
metrics can be considered and some of them (its objectives) are conflict-
ing (see Section 2.1.1), it is necessary to define a dominance operator
that allows to compare the behavior produced by two different setups
in order to determine the best wrapper version. Moreover, since the
wrapper is a stochastic process, it must be run several times to obtain
sample distributions of all its behavioral metrics (see Section 2.6). There-
fore, this dominance criterion must be supported by statistical tests
to ensure that if the behavior of one setup dominates that of another,
it is because there are statistically significant differences between the
sample distributions following each of the metrics for the two setups
being compared.


3.3 conclusions
75
3.2.4.2
Objective O4.2: Definition of a ranking-based score to compare mul-
tiple wrapper configurations
The optimization of the wrapper requires a procedure that allows the
comparison of its behavior with multiple configurations for a given
metric. Thus, this specific objective aims to develop a scalar score that
allows the complete sorting of multiple wrapper configurations for
a given metric. The absolute difference of this score metric for two
different configurations must reflect the magnitude of the statistical
difference of the sample distributions of a given behavioral metric
obtained with such configurations.
3.3
conclusions
Following the comprehensive examination of evolutionary wrappers for
high-dimensional FS problems presented in Chapter 2, three challenges
have been identified: the mitigation of the NSGA-II’s FNDS method
bottleneck, the acceleration of the wrapper convergence through a de-
crease in the average size of individuals in the initial population, and
the optimization of the wrapper’s migration hyperparameters. These
challenges have led to the formulation of Hypotheses H1, H2, and
H3, which propose feasible solutions to these challenges. In order to
confirm these hypotheses, a series of general and specific objectives
have been defined. Besides, additional objectives, such as the devel-
opment of an evolutionary wrapper to serve as the basis for future
implementations and the definition of statistical procedures to ensure
accurate comparison of the behavior of different wrapper alternatives,
are also necessary to successfully address these challenges. With this in
mind, the following part of the thesis, which includes Chapters 4 to 6,
present the methodology proposed to address each of these objectives.

Before proceeding with the FS phase, it is imperative to ensure that the

4.2 data pre-processing
81
method for properly pre-processing the datasets analyzed along this
dissertation, which can be found in Appendix B. Since all the datasets
are labeled, they can be framed within supervised classification.
As discussed in Section 1.1.3, the pre-processing phase consists of 3
sub-steps: data cleaning, data integration, and data scaling. However, the
second one, which is only necessary to create a new dataset from data
coming from different sources, can be skipped, since all the datasets
analyzed in this thesis are already well defined.
Regarding data cleaning, different strategies have been proposed in the
literature for the detection of outliers [273]. However, one of the most
widely used methodologies is a technique known as majority voting
[274, 275], in which several methods are used and a sample is discarded
if the majority of them detect it as an outlier. The choice of the number
of methods used depends on the study, but it has been proven that
three is an adequate option [276, 277].
The next step is to select the three methods to perform outlier clean-
ing, which can be developed in-house or chosen from any ML library.
In this regard, Scikit-learn offers three methods: IsolationForest [278],
LocalOutlierFactor [279], and OneClassSVM [280]. The effectiveness of
these methods in identifying outliers has been demonstrated in numer-
ous studies [281–285], making them a suitable option for use in this
process.
Using the above data cleaning methodology, samples significantly far
from the mean are detected as outliers. Nevertheless, there may remain
samples that are considered "minioutliers" and may affect the data
scaling step [286]. With this in mind, the RobustScaler method proposed
in [287], which uses the IQR to normalize data and is also robust to
IQR: InterQuartile
Range
outliers, is a good choice for the data scaling phase.
In light of the aforementioned considerations, Algorithm 4.1 illustrates
the pseudocode of the pre-processing methodology developed. The three
selected outlier detection methods generate a vector of estimates, one
for each sample (Lines 2 to 4). Each estimate can be negative or positive,
indicating that its corresponding sample is or is not detected as an
outlier. Once this step is complete, all the estimate vectors are iterated.
For those samples identified as outliers, the value of the outlier counter
is incremented by 1. Subsequently, if the value of this counter is less
than 2, indicating that the majority of detectors has not identified the
sample as an outlier, it is integrated into the preprocessed dataset
(Line 16). Finally, the RobusScaler function is used to carry out the data
scaling phase.

4.3.1
Search engine and classification method
As discussed in Section 2.1.1, FS problems are commonly treated as
MOOPs. Despite the numerous EAs that have been proposed for this
type of optimization, NSGA-II has emerged as one of the most relevant
(see Section 2.1.3.1), primarily due to its crowded-comparison operator
(≺c), which favors elitism while maintaining diversity. Thus, NSGA-II
has been chosen as the search engine.
Regarding the classification method, k-NN has been chosen as the
preferred option to evaluate each of the potential solutions due to its
versatility and effectiveness (see Section 2.3).
4.3.2
Particularization for high-dimensional FS problems
An EA-based wrapper has proven to be an excellent solution for FS
problems (see Section 2.1). However, MOEW is designed to tackle FS


84
4 base procedures design
problems in high-dimensional spaces, so each of its component must
be tailored to ensure optimal performance.
4.3.2.1
k-NN implementation
Different implementations of k-NN have been developed over the years
to improve its efficiency as the dataset size grows (see Section 2.3.3).
However, these do not seem to be suitable for high-dimensional FS
problems, in which brute force k-NN is recommended when n f > 15
(see Section 2.4.2). Anyway, as discussed in that section, Scikit-learn
enables the automatic selection of the optimal version of k-NN based
on the dataset, effectively addressing this issue.
4.3.2.2
Fitness function
As stated in Section 2.1.1, the two objectives optimized in FS problems
involves minimizing the number of selected features while maximizing
classifier efficacy. The former is measured directly by counting the
number of features selected by the individual. On the other hand, there
are numerous metrics that can be used to estimate the latter. However,
the Kappa index has been chosen because it has proven to be one of
the most robust metrics, mainly because it takes into account not only
the accuracy of the classifier but also the per-class error distribution
(see Section 2.1.1).
An important issue to estimate the classifier efficacy is to avoid over-
fitting, whereby the final classification model is strongly correlated
with the training dataset information. MOEW uses CVDOG to address
this problem, considering the discussion in Section 2.1.10. Basically,
CVDOG splits the training dataset into two stratified subsets (training
and validation) for the evaluation of each individual according to the
pv hyperparameter, performing a sort of cross-validation distributed
over the generations of the wrapper procedure. In addition to avoiding
overfitting, this approach reduces the computational cost considerably
compared to traditional cross-validation, which splits the dataset into
different training and validation partitions for each evaluation.


4.3 multi-objective evolutionary wrapper
85
4.3.2.3
Individual representation
As stated in Section 2.1.4, a binary representation may be a possible
approach in the context of FS problems. However, this type of rep-
resentation has the significant disadvantage of the high amount of
memory needed to store the unselected features. In this regard, the
integer representation proposed in [90] and detailed in Section 2.1.4
has been chosen, in which individuals are composed of a subset of
indexes of the selected features. The use of sets is driven by the aim of
avoiding the repetition of selected features in individuals. While this
representation involves the use of more complex breeding operators, it
is more efficient in terms of resource consumption.
4.3.2.4
Breeding operators
Breeding operators must be designed according to the individual rep-
resentation, in order to produce valid solutions for the problem. In
this sense, MOEW uses the operators developed in [90], extensively
detailed in Sections 2.1.5 and 2.1.6, since they are specifically designed
to work with subsets of selected features.
Briefly, the crossover operator replicates the features common to the
parents of the two offspring, while features different from both parents
are randomly distributed into descendants. This ensures that valid
individuals with the same size as the parents are always generated. For
the mutation operator, each feature has a probability of pind of being
affected, thereby determining the subset of features to be removed or
either replaced by a new one.
4.3.2.5
Parent and survival selection mechanisms
On the one hand, the parent selection mechanism is based on a stochastic
binary tournament selection because it has been shown to work well
in EAs, as described in Section 2.1.9. Since MOOPs are addressed, the
≺d operator is responsible for selecting the dominant individual (see
Section 2.1.2.1), i.e., the one which wins the tournament. In the event
of non-dominated solutions, one is chosen randomly.
On the other hand, the NSGA-II’s survivor selection mechanism con-
siders the union of the parent and offspring populations and select


86
4 base procedures design
the best ni individuals according to the ≺c operator, as detailed in
Section 2.1.3.1.
4.3.2.6
Stop criterion
Two options have been provided to stop the evolution of the procedure.
On the one hand, MOEW can be configured to stop after a specific
number of generations (ng). On the other hand, an adaptive stop cri-
terion that analyzes the convergence of the algorithm over the last ga
generations can be adopted. Specifically, the convergence is determined
by two criteria:
• Intra-generation convergence in the last ga generations. This
criterion is designed to assess whether all individuals within a
given population exhibit comparable classifier efficacy over the
span of the last ga generations. This analysis aims to evaluate
the stability of the population under examination. Therefore,
the population individuals’ Kappa index standard deviation (sk)
should be below the intra-generation convergence threshold (skth)
throughout each one of the last ga generations.
• Inter-generation convergence in the last ga generations. While
the aforementioned criterion determines whether the individuals
in the population demonstrate stability in each ga generation,
it does not assess how the population’s mean Kappa index (¯k)
evolves, which should be similar to detect convergence. So, the
difference between the ¯k obtained in the first and last of these
ga generations should be lower than the inter-generation conver-
gence threshold (¯kth).
As previously noted, this stop criterion does not take the second ob-
jective of the wrapper (number of selected features) into account to
determine when to halt the procedure. The rationale for this approach
is that it has been considered preferable to prioritize solutions with the
highest possible Kappa index, even if it means a slight increase in the
number of selected features, over solutions with fewer features but a
lower Kappa index. Once the Kappa index of the solutions has reached
a point of convergence, it falls upon the DM to select those that align
most closely with the study’s requirements.
It is important to recall the risk that the wrapper may not be able
to meet the stop criteria within a reasonable time, as mentioned in
Section 2.1.11. In such cases, it is recommended to set a maximum

as a means of specifying this value.
This novel stop criterion has been presented at the international GECCO

4.3.3
Hyperparameter configuration
The operation of MOEW is determined by the hyperparameters that
regulate its behavior. In this sense, the different heuristics adopted to
adjust each of them are detailed below:
• Adaptive stop criterion. ga, mg, skth, and ¯kth have been adjusted
to strike a balance between avoiding premature convergence and
continuing the search once MOEW has converged. A series of trial
and error experiments with several datasets revealed that high
values of ga, skth, and ¯kth resulted in stagnation at local optima, as
the search process was ceased prematurely before convergencing.
Conversely, when ga, skth, and ¯kth were set to low values, con-
vergence was not uncovered after thousands of generations. In
this context, ga= 15, skth= 0.1, and ¯kth= 0.01 seem to be appro-
priate values for these three hyperparameters, since the average
number of generations required to obtain appropriate solutions
ranged from 100 to 600 for all datasets. However, due to the
stochastic nature of MOEW, the search was sometimes extended
up to several thousand generations without an improvement in
results. To avoid unnecessary expenditure of time and resources,
a maximum number of generations mg = 1000 has been set.
• Number of neighbors for k-NN (k). Following the discussion in
Section 2.3.2, the heuristic presented in [225] has been adopted,
in which k takes the nearest odd value of the square root of ns.
Although this heuristic may require slightly more execution time
than setting k to 5, it is less prone to overfitting.
• Number of individuals (ni). Although ni should be set to a value
close to n f , as stated in Section 2.1.8, DEAP requires the number
of individuals to be a multiple of 4 [288]. Since both conditions

as:

• Number of executions (ne). The number of executions has been

• Percentage of training data destined for validation (pv). Accord-
ing to the empirical study performed in [127], the percentage
of samples used for validation when applying CVDOG (see Sec-

while reducing the training time and avoiding the overfitting.
• Probability of applying the crossover operator (pc). As described
in Section 2.1.7, a suitable value for this hyperparameter seems
to be 0.8.
• Probability to select a individual to mutate (pm). As stated in

• Probability that a feature mutates independently of the others

4.5

Once MOEW is proposed, its behavior should be evaluated. This be-
havior is not only related to its objectives, which estimate the quality
of the results it finds, but some other metrics could be used, such
as its execution time or the energy it consumes. Thus, some kind of
dominance criterion is needed to compare MOEW’s behavior, based on
such metrics, with that of other wrapper alternatives (Objective O4.1).
Also, since MOEW is a stochastic process, a sample distribution of
all the metrics used to estimate its behavior should be used to make
the comparison (see Section 2.6). Therefore, the dominance criterion
should be defined to compare the behavior of MOEW according to
sample distributions of multiple behavior metrics. This dominance
criterion can then be used to compare the performance of MOEW with
that of other state-of-the-art wrappers over several low-, medium-, and
high-dimensional datasets (Objective O1.3).

4.6
conclusions
In this chapter, all issues concerning the development of a base evolu-
tionary wrapper (MOEW) that can successfully solve high-dimensional
FS problems have been addressed as a part of Objective O1. First, a
data pre-processing methodology has been proposed (Objective O1.1)
to ensure that the datasets are free of impurities, allowing MOEW
to achieve appropriate results. Second, the development framework
to implement MOEW has been defined. Then, each part of MOEW,
which uses NSGA-II as its search strategy and k-NN as its classification
method, has been tailored to address high-dimensional FS problems
(Objective O1.2). Finally, the behavior of MOEW must be evaluated in
comparison with other relevant wrappers in the literature to assess its
efficacy (Objective O1.3). To this end, a dominance criterion has been
put forth to facilitate comparisons between two wrapper alternatives
according to sample distributions of multiple performance metrics (Ob-
jective O4.1). This criterion can also be used to evaluate the behavior of
MOEW with different hyperparameter configurations, which is very
useful to achieve Objectives O2 and O3, which will be approached in
the following chapters.
The behavior of MOEW is assessed in Chapter 7, showing that MOEW
can obtain feature subsets for a wide variety of FS problems that can
compete with or even outperform several relevant wrappers in the
recent literature.
Once MOEW has been developed, the next chapter sets out the proce-
dures that address Objective O2, with the aim of improving its efficiency.
As Hypothesis H1 postulated, the main bottleneck of MOEW for high-
dimensional FS problems (the NSGA-II’s FNDS method) should be
mitigated with the development of a multi-population model. However,
since FS problems are treated as MOOPs, a novel migration policy must
be developed to consider this issue (Objective O2.1). It can then be used
in both the sequential multi-population model (Objective O2.2) and
its subsequent parallel approach to accelerate MOEW (Objective O2.3).
Finally, the possibility of reducing the average size of the individuals in
the initial population to boost the convergence is explored (Objective
O2.4).

5.1
migration process
As discussed in Section 2.2.1, an appropriate adjustment of the migra-
tion process is essential for a multi-population model to work correctly.
This process facilitates the promotion of genetic diversity among sub-
populations through the exchange of individuals at regular intervals.
This section therefore addresses the configuration of the migration for
any multi-population approach of MOEW.
Typically, the migration process is governed by six hyperparameters:
mi, mr, mp, mt, nsp, and ssp (see Section 2.2.1.1). A multi-population
model is constituted by nsp subpopulations, each comprising ssp indi-
viduals. The migration process occurs every mi generations, whereby
mr individuals are transferred from the source subpopulation to the


5.1 migration process
95
destination one. These transfers are conducted in accordance with the
topology proposed by mt. Ultimately, the selection of individuals to
migrate and their integration into the destination subpopulation are
determined by mp.

Since the optimization of the migration hyperparameters in the context
of high-dimensional FS problems is part of Objective O3, discussed
in Chapter 6, they have been provisionally adjusted according to the
classical recommendations (see Section 2.2.1.2) to validate the multi-
population approaches of MOEW.
Firstly, in accordance with the guidelines set out by Cantú-Paz and
Tomassini, mi = 15 and mr = 0.1. Secondly, it is essential to consider
the ni adjustment, which should to be equal to n f and be a multiple of
4 to meet the DEAP restriction on population size (see Section 4.3.3),
to tune ssp. In this context, ssp = ⌈(n f /nsp)/4⌉× 4, as individuals are
distributed into subpopulations in accordance with Tanese’s scheme
(see Section 2.2). In contrast, nsp does not have a default value, since it
may depend on the size of the problem or the number of CPU cores
in which the parallel procedure (described later in Section 5.4.1.2) is
executed, as long as ssp is not too small, as recommended by Cantú-Paz
(see Section 2.2.1.2). Therefore, the number of subpopulations is left
to be adjusted depending on the experiment performed. Regarding
mt, an Uni-directional Ring topology has been selected because Ru-

Finally, the best-worst policy has been chosen for mp because it seems

5.2
elitist probabilistic migration policy
Since high-dimensional FS problems are treated as MOOPs, and the
population consists of a considerable number of individuals (see Sec-
tion 2.1.8), it is essential to adapt the best-worst policy to address this
issue. In this sense, the aim is to select the best migrants of the source
subpopulation Pi from its Pareto front F0(Pi) to favor elitism and re-
duce the number of potential migrants (see Section 2.2.1.4). Figure 5.1
shows the flow chart of this novel migration policy, which is explained
in more detail below.
Typically, hyperparameter mr, which remains constant throughout
the evolutionary process, determines the number of migrants chosen
from the source subpopulation. However, a policy based on selecting
individuals from F0(Pi) depends on its variable size in each generation.
To address this and streamline the process, a new hyperparameter ml is
proposed to replace mr. It is defined as the likelihood that one Pareto-


5.3 sequential multi-population moew
97
optimal solution becomes a migrant. Since all F0(Pi) members have
an ml probability of being selected as migrants, the average number
of selected migrants (nm) depends on both the generation and the
subpopulation. It can be estimated as:
nmij = ml × |F0j(Pi)|
(5.1)
in which |F0j(Pi)| is the number of Pareto-optimal solutions of the
i −th subpopulation at generation j.
It could be the case that no migrant is selected, whether because of a
low value of ml or |F0j(Pi)|. In this improbable scenario, a randomly
selected solution from the Pareto Front is chosen as a migrant to avoid
the performance degradation caused by running the subpopulations in
isolation, as described in Section 2.2.1.2.
Finally, when the migrants arrive at the destination subpopulation, they
are added to the population. Later, the survival selection mechanism

5.4
parallelization of the multi-population model
Since each subpopulation of SMP-MOEW evolves independently, ex-
changing information only during the migration process, Objective
O2.3 proposes to continue accelerating the procedure through parallel
programming. In this sense, this section tackles this issue by developing
a parallel multicore scheme with asynchronous migrations for UMA
architectures (hereinafter referred to as PMP-MOEW), whose design
can be found in Figure 5.2. In essence, the new procedure entails that
each CPU core is responsible for managing the evolution of a single
subpopulation. Thus, the new complexity order of FNDS is O(no ·
(ni/nsp)2)), instead of the O((no · ni2)/nsp) for SMP-MOEW, since
each subpopulation is executed in parallel.

5.4.1
Python implementation
Since, as outlined in Section 4.1, Python has been selected for the
development of the procedures presented in this dissertation, this
section details the implementation of PMP-MOEW in this language.
5.4.1.1
Parallel execution of the subpopulations
During the development of this thesis, the Python interpreter remains
unable to be controlled by more than one thread at a time due to its
GIL 1 (see Section 2.4.1). In this context, the Multiprocessing library
[254] provides a means of achieving parallelism in Python by creating
multiple processes that can be executed simultaneously on different
cores. However, even though thread-based parallelism is typically more
efficient than process-based parallelism, as discussed in Section 1.4.3,
parallelizing MOEW through processes should not add significant
overhead to PMP-MOEW execution because all subpopulations evolve
independently and occasional migrations are implemented through
asynchronous communication.
With this in mind, considering the PMP-MOEW design illustrated in
Figure 5.2, the multiprocessing approach is described as follows. The
parent process (P0) creates as many processes as there are subpopula-
tions and waits for all the child processes to finish. Communication
between subpopulations occurs only during the migration process. As
with the majority of programming languages, the Multiprocessing library
offers two options to perform this communication: Pipe and Queue. The
former is the most efficient option but is designed for simple data
and point-to-point communication between two subprocesses. In this
context, the Queue class is a more suitable choice as it allows commu-
nication between multiple processes and supports more complex data
structures, such as individuals. In accordance with the Uni-directional
Ring topology outlined in Section 5.1.1, a queue must be established for
each pair of subpopulations. For more detailed information on which
functions of this library are used, as well as a brief overview of the
Multiprocessing library, please refer to Appendix E.3.
1 In mid-2024, version 3.13 of Python was released, which allows users to disable GIL,
although it is still an experimental feature.

5.4.1.2
Maximum number of subpopulations
It is important to highlight that the number of subpopulations, nsp,
should not be greater than the number of physical cores of the CPU in
which PMP-MOEW is executed.
5.4.1.3
Interaction between Scikit-learn and Multiprocessing modules
As discussed in Section 4.1, Scikit-learn has been chosen as the ML
library to develop k-NN, which is used to evaluate each of the wrapper
solutions. It should be remembered that Scikit-learn relies on Numpy to
execute its numerical computations, which in turn uses the BLAS and
LAPACK linear algebra routines, implemented by external libraries
such as MKL, OpenBLAS, or BLIS, which are designed to utilize all
available logical cores by default, as discussed in Section 2.4.2.
This design, which allows Scikit-learn to be computationally efficient,
has not caused any issues yet because all the procedures described
so far are sequential. Nevertheless, it drastically reduces the efficiency
of parallel wrapper implementations for multicore CPUs. Given that
the evolution of each subpopulation is managed by a different pro-
cess, which is executed on a different physical core, it is inadvisable
to allow each instance of Scikit-learn’s k-NN execution to use all the
logical cores. Doing so would create a major contention problem, which
would significantly reduce the efficiency of PMP-MOEW because all
cores are already running PMP-MOEW. It is therefore mandatory that
each instance of k-NN utilizes only a single physical core. As stated in
Section 2.4.2, BLAS and LAPACK provide the MKL_NUM_THREADS,
OPENBLAS_NUM_THREADS, and BLIS_NUM_THREADS environ-
ment variables to modify this behaviour, which should be set 1 to
ensure that k-NN is run only on the core that executes the subpopula-
tion to be evaluated.

Hypothesis H2 postulated the possibility of decreasing the value of p f
to speed up convergence, since using the commonly used value of 0.5

the lowest possible value of p f while maintaining the quality of the

criterion is then used in a binary search (Section 5.5.1) to identify the

The minimum p f value found by the binary search proposed in Sec-

5.6
conclusions
This chapter outlines a series of procedures designed to enhance the
efficiency of MOEW (Objective O2). However, prior to proceeding
with the development of the multi-population model that addresses
Hypothesis H1, it has been necessary to propose a migration policy that
is adapted to MOOPs (Objective O2.1), which is the type of optimization
used for FS problems. This novel policy considers the variable size of
the Pareto front in each generation, rather than the entire population.
Thus, a new hyperparameter ml, defined as the probability that each
individual belonging to the Pareto front could become a migrant, has
replaced mr. Subsequently, a sequential multi-population model (SMP-
MOEW) has been proposed to reduce the algorithmic complexity of
the NSGA-II’s FNDS method by a factor of nsp, answering Objective
O2.2.
Next, given that each subpopulation in SMP-MOEW evolves inde-
pendently, SMP-MOEW has been upgraded to PMP-MOEW, a new
parallel multi-population MOEW published in [290] in which each
CPU core is dedicated to the evolution of a single subpopulation using
a multiprocessing approach, whose migration process is performed
asynchronously to avoid any stall in the execution flow of each subpop-
ulation (Objective O2.3).


106
5 wrapper optimizations
The last optimization of MOEW is related to the reduction in the
average size of the initial population individuals, which is regulated by
hyperparameter p f (Objective O2.4). A binary search-based procedure
has been proposed to find the lowest value of p f that ensures the
quality of the solutions generated by the wrapper. It is expected that
the number of generations required by the wrapper to converge will
decrease as p f is reduced. This can be readily verified by inspecting the
different values of p f evaluated by the binary search and the number
of generations needed by the wrapper to converge with each one.
The next chapter presents a methodology to test the feasibility of the
classical recommendations for tuning the migration process when ad-
dressing high-dimensional FS problems (Objective O3). First, the impact
of the population partitioning scheme on the efficacy of PMP-MOEW
(Objective O3.1) is analyzed, which is likely to converge prematurely
to local optima as ssp decreases. Therefore, Objective O3.2 aims to find
an optimal population partitioning scheme (nspmax,sspmin) that allows
the wrapper to escape from local optima while minimizing resource
consumption. Finally, the influence of the remaining migration hyper-
parameters on PMP-MOEW using the optimal population partitioning
scheme is analyzed (Objective O3.3).

Before proceeding with this chapter, it is important to recall the
objectives that have been addressed so far. First, a base multi-
objective EA-based wrapper (MOEW) was developed to adequately
solve high-dimensional FS problems (Objective O1), whose behavior
can be evaluated, in comparison with other state-of-the-art wrappers,
thanks to the dominance criterion proposed in response to Objective
O4.1, which facilitates the comparison between two wrapper alterna-
tives according to sample distributions of multiple behavioral metrics.
However, MOEW had significant room for improvement in terms of
efficiency, so Objective O2 addressed this issue. The primary bottleneck
for high-dimensional FS problems in MOEW was the NSGA-II’s FNDS
method. In this regard, Hypothesis H1 proposed a solution in the form
of a multi-population model. However, since FS problems are treated
as MOOPs, a novel migration policy, tailored to this type of optimiza-
tion, was initially developed (Objective O2.1). Subsequently, it was
incorporated into the multi-population model (Objective O2.2), which
was upgraded to a multicore parallel scheme for UMA architectures,
resulting in PMP-MOEW (Objective O2.3). Here, each subpopulation
evolves independently on each CPU core, exchanging information asyn-
chronously and only in the migration process. Finally, a method to
minimize the value of p f , also based on the aforementioned dominance
criterion, was proposed to reduce the average size of the individuals
in the initial population in order to improve the convergence of the
wrapper (Objective O2.4).

In light of the aforementioned considerations, this chapter addresses
the methodology to satisfy Objective O3. Firstly, both the migration
hyperparameters analyzed and the metrics considered are outlined in
Sections 6.1 and 6.2, respectively. Next, Section 6.3 proposes a procedure
to analyze the relevance of the population partitioning scheme (nsp,
ssp) on the PMP-MOEW behavior. Since the entire population of ni
individuals is to be divided into nsp subpopulations, the subpopulation
size, ssp, decreases as nsp increases. Thus, there should be a point in
which PMP-MOEW prematurely converges due to the small number of
individuals per subpopulation. To perform this study, many migration
hyperparameter configurations must be analyzed. Therefore, a scalar
score that allows a multiple comparison of the sample distributions
obtained with multiple configurations for a given behavioral metric
(Objective O4.2) is proposed in Section 6.4. Then, in Section 6.5, a
procedure is proposed to find an optimal population partition scheme
(nspmax, sspmin) so that the wrapper is able to escape from local optima
while minimizing resource consumption (Objective O3.2). Finally, once
the optimal population partitioning scheme has been identified, the
remaining migration hyperparameters must be studied to determine
their influence on the behavior of PMP-MOEW in Section 6.6 (Objective
O3.3).
The procedures proposed in this chapter are experimentally verified in
Chapter 9 using several high-dimensional datasets.
6.1
hyperparameters analyzed
It should be noted that not all the hyperparameters that regulate the
migration process require analysis. As discussed in Section 2.2.1.4, it
is not recommended to pursue further investigation of hyperparame-
ters mt and mp. Therefore, they will remain at their default values of
Uni-directional Ring (Section 5.1.1) and elitist probabilistic migration
(Section 5.2), respectively.
With this in mind, the hyperparameters under consideration are mi, ml,
nsp, and ssp, as there is currently no existing work that addresses the
study of each of them and their interactions when using large popu-
lations, such as those needed to solve high-dimensional FS problems
(see Section 2.1.8).

Several metrics are obtained from each execution to make possible the
analysis of the PMP-MOEW performance concerning its hyperparame-

multi-objective problems are solved, each execution provides several
Pareto-optimal solutions. Thus, the average value of each objective for
the Pareto front solutions are used since in this way the average quality

execution time and energy consumption should be also measured to

the configuration), the score proposed in (6.9) provides better inter-
pretability because its values are always defined in [0, 1), independently
of the number of compared hyperparameter configurations.
Finally, for those configurations that yield statistically different results
for a given metric, i.e., a different score, the effect size should be
calculated to estimate the magnitude of such differences. The effect
size obtained should correlate with the score differences obtained.
Specifically, Cohen’s d has been used in this work.


6.5 optimization of the population partitioning scheme
113
6.5
optimization of the population partitioning scheme
The procedure outlined in Section 6.3 to address Objective O3.1 should
show a tendency for PMP-MOEW to converge prematurely as the size
of subpopulations (ssp) decreases. Thus, the next step is to determine
an optimal population partitioning scheme (nspmax, sspmin) that prevents
the search from stalling at local optima and also minimizes the resource
consumption (Objective O3.2).
An analysis of the quality of solutions as ssp decreases and nsp increases
should identify a point between two successive population partition-
ing
schemes, (nspj, sspj) and (nspj+1, sspj+1) , with nspj > nspj+1 and
sspj < sspj+1, in which the degradation begins to be noticeable, i.e.,
premature convergence should be observed when using a subpopu-
lation size of sspj, but not when using sspj+1. Therefore, the minimum
value of ssp that maintains the quality of the solutions, sspmin, should
be in the interval [sspj, sspj+1]. This interval must be searched with nspj
subpopulations because scheme (nspj, sspj) has shown a clear tendency
to converge prematurely. It is expected that increasing the subpopula-
tion size from sspj to sspmin could prevent premature convergence when
using nspj subpopulations. Finally, the procedure should be performed
independently for each dataset, as the value of sspmin may vary from
dataset to dataset.
As an exhaustive search in the [sspj, sspj+1] interval is rather costly,
a binary search-based approach has been proposed, which features
several modifications regarding the original algorithm [291]. However,
before proceeding with a detailed examination of this procedure, it is
important to highlight four crucial aspects:
• The purpose of determining the value of sspmin is to identify a
minimum threshold for the subpopulation size that enables the
maintenance of solution quality, which is measured by the two
objectives optimized by PMP-MOEW. In this sense, the scores of
both the average test Kappa index (K) and the average number
of selected features (NF) are considered to guide the search.
Nevertheless, sample distributions of the other efficiency-related
metrics (execution time, T, and energy consumption, E) are also
obtained because although not used now, they will be used later
to confirm the value of nspmax.
• Each time a new subpopulation size is evaluated, the scores of
all the previously evaluated subpopulation sizes must be recalcu-

previous scores.
• Two score values are considered similar based on the following
similarity criterion:
s(MWa) ≈s(MWb) ⇔|s(MWa) −s(MWb)| < sth
(6.10)

As with the adjustment of α in parametric and non-parametric
tests, an adjustment should be made according to the desired
precision for the score similarity. In this sense, a value of 0.05
might be an appropriate choice.
• The evaluation of each possible value for sspmin is quite costly.
Specifically, the number of different wrapper configurations eval-

nC = |MI| × |ML|

each new subpopulation size to be analyzed. Therefore, the search
could be stopped if the interval to be searched is too narrow, since
the possible change in sspmin is not worth the computational cost.
This premature stopping criterion is regulated by the wth hyper-
parameter, a threshold for the minimum width of the interval.
Since the total population size depends on the number of features
in the dataset, wth should be adjusted considering this matter.
This value should be low enough to achieve a balance between
resource consumption and the desired precision for the sspmin
fit, but not too low, since analyzing very small intervals would
not result in a notable change for the value of sspmin, despite the
extensive number of executions required to perform a new grid

117
Confirming nspmax is straightforward, and no further runs of the wrap-
per are needed, since all the new population partitioning schemes
have already been evaluated to validate sspmin. In fact, the grid search
provides four distributions of behavioral metrics (for the average test
Kappa index, the average number of features, the computation time,
and the energy consumed) for each population partitioning scheme,
as discussed previously. The scores of the first two have already been
used to verify sspmin. Therefore, the only remaining task is to calculate
and compare the scores for the efficiency-related metrics. Since all
partitioning schemes with nsp ≥nspj now have ssp = sspmin, their scores
for both computation time and energy consumed should be worse than
those of (nspmax, sspmin).

of migrants
Once the optimal population partitioning scheme (nspmax, sspmin) has
been identified for each dataset, it can be used to analyze the influence
of mi and ml, providing an answer to Objective O3.3. Again, no further
runs of the wrapper are required because all the combinations of
MI and ML values have already been evaluated for the population
partitioning scheme (nspmax, sspmin). However, the samples of every
behavioral metric must now be grouped into different distributions,
each corresponding to each possible (mi, ml) combination. Then, the
scores of these new sample distributions can be calculated for the four
behavioral metrics, which allows an assessment of the influence of mi
and ml on the behavior of PMP-MOEW.
6.7
conclusions
This chapter has put forth a methodology to address Objective O3 and
optimize the hyperparameters that regulate the migration process for
high-dimensional FS problems. First of all, the hyperparameters to be
analyzed have been determined, concluding that mt and mp should not
be included in the study and should be left at their default values. Thus,
only mi, ml, nsp, and ssp should be considered. Furthermore, in order
to assess the performance of PMP-MOEW, the following four metrics
have been considered: average test Kappa index, average number of
selected features, execution time, and energy consumption.


118
6 migration process tuning for high-dimensional fs problems
Then, a procedure has been proposed to evaluate the impact of the
population partitioning scheme on the effectiveness of PMP-MOEW
(Objective O3.1). Many samples of the four behavioral metrics under
consideration must be generated with a grid search for all the possible
combinations of the values of mi, ml, and the population partitioning
schemes (nsp, ssp). These samples can be then grouped into distributions
according to their partitioning scheme, in order to allow the comparison
of the wrapper behavior for different partitioning schemes. Then, a
ranking of the population partitioning schemes can be performed for
the average test Kappa index and the average number of features,
which is useful to detect premature convergence as the subpopulation
size decreases. A new score metric has been developed to enable the
ranking of multiple sample distributions for a given metric (Objective
O4.2).
PMP-MOEW should show a tendency to converge prematurely as
the subpopulation size decreases. Therefore, a method has been pro-
posed to identify a minimum subpopulation size sspmin that avoids
this behavior. Once this minimum subpopulation size threshold has
been estimated, all population partitioning schemes can be corrected
so that ssp ≥sspmin, which should prevent premature convergence for
all schemes. Then, a maximum threshold for the number of subpop-
ulations, nspmax, can also be determined to minimize the wrapper’s
resource consumption.
Finally, the optimal population partitioning scheme (nspmax, sspmin) can
be used to determine the influence of mi and ml on the PMP-MOEW
behavior by using the scores of each pair of values (mi, ml) for all four
metrics (Objective O3.3).
All of the procedures presented in this chapter have been applied
to several datasets in Chapter 9. Furthermore, this chapter fulfills
the methodological part of this dissertation, addressing each of the
objectives set out in Chapter 3. Therefore, the next part presents the
experimental results.

In Chapter 4, MOEW was proposed as a multi-objective evolutionary
wrapper capable of adequately addressing high-dimensional FS
problems (Objective O1). Furthermore, a methodology was presented
in Section 4.5 to evaluate the behavior of MOEW compared to other

according to sample distributions of multiple performance metrics.
Since the aim of this chapter is to assess the quality of the solutions

possible to find a set of wrappers with comparable metrics that analyze

This chapter presents the experimental results that validate the vari-
ous optimizations proposed in Chapter 5, in response to Objective
O2, to improve the efficiency of MOEW. First, the Elitist Probabilistic
migration policy defined in Section 5.2 is validated in Section 8.1 by
comparing it to the two most commonly used policies in the literature:
the best-worst and random-random policies. Then, Section 8.2.1 confirms
that the NSGA-II’s FNDS method generates a significant bottleneck
when using a single population to address high-dimensional FS prob-
lems. Subsequently, Section 8.2.2 shows how this bottleneck can be
alleviated by the multi-population model of MOEW, SMP-MOEW,
proposed in Section 5.3. Then, the results achieved by PMP-MOEW,
a parallel version of SMP-MOEW described in Section 5.4, are pre-
sented in Section 8.3, showing a great improvement in the efficiency
of the wrapper. Finally, Section 8.4 shows how the average length of
the individuals in the initial population, regulated by p f , affects the
wrapper convergence, confirming Hypothesis H2, i.e., as p f is lowered,
the number of generations needed to converge also decreases.
Before starting any of the aforementioned experiments, it is essential
to highlight the following point. The hyperparameters related to the
migration process (see Section 5.1) are set according to the specific
experiment to be performed, since they depend on the problem to be

validation of the elitist probabilistic migration pol-
icy
Before starting with the results of the different MOEW optimizations, it
is worth comparing the performance of the novel migration policy pre-
sented in Section 5.2 with that of the two most commonly used policies
in the literature: the best-worst and random-random policies (see Sec-
tion 2.2.1.2). For this purpose, it is important to remember the difficulty
of selecting the best individuals from a subpopulation when solving
MOOPs (see Section 2.2.1.4). Indeed, this issue motivates the develop-
ment of the Elitist Probabilistic migration (see Section 5.2). However, this
problem is not common to all multi-objective evolutionary methods.
In the case of NSGA-II, which is the basis of MOEW, the crowding
distance (see Section 2.1.3.1) allows the sorting of the individuals within
each front of non-dominated solutions, leading to a completely ordered
population. In this case, applying the best-worst policy, as originally
defined by Cantú-Paz (see Section 2.2.1.2), is straightforward. For other
multi-objective evolutionary procedures, an adaptation of the method,
such as the one proposed in this dissertation, is required.
The experiment was performed using SMP-MOEW. Its migration hyper-
parameters were adjusted through a trial-and-error process to achieve
the best possible configuration. Specifically, nsp = 16, ssp = 300, and mi
= 5. For the Elitist Probabilistic migration, ml was set to 0.3 as described
above. This value was also used for mr when applying the best-worst
and random-random policies. SMP-MOEW was run ne = 30 times for
500 generations for the 104, 107, and 110 Essex datasets, detailed in
Appendix B.2, and each migration policy. In brief, each dataset is split
into training and test data, consisting of 178 samples and 3 600 features
each.

datasets. It can be observed that the new proposed migration policy
and the best-worst policy obtain similar results for both the average
test Kappa index and the average number of selected features, while
