8.2
nsga-ii’s fnds bottleneck mitigation through a multi-
population approach
Since the algorithmic complexity of FNDS is O(no · ni2) (see Sec-
tion 2.1.3.1) and ni ≈n f for FS problems (see Section 2.1.8), the FNDS


8.2 nsga-ii’s fnds bottleneck mitigation
133
method of NSGA-II causes a significant bottleneck for large popula-
tions, as experimentally confirmed in Section 8.2.1. However, this issue
can be solved by distributing individuals across subpopulations, as
SMP-MOEW does. Section 8.2.2 confirms that the time spent on the
FNDS method decreases linearly as the number of subpopulations
increases, confirming Hypothesis H1.
8.2.1
Magnitude of the NSGA-II’s FNDS method bottleneck
Initially, it is important to quantify the magnitude of the NSGA-II’s
FNDS method bottleneck when addressing high-dimensional FS prob-
lems. For this propose, MOEW has been executed using the 104, 107,
and 110 Essex datasets. Initially, the adaptive stop criterion described in
Section 4.3.2.6 was employed to determine the precise number of gener-
ations required to achieve convergence, which are 398, 466, and 470 for
subjects 104, 107, and 110, respectively. Finally, MOEW was launched
ne = 30 times using this number of generations for each dataset. From
this process, the average times of solutions evaluation, FNDS method,
and the rest of the functions of MOEW were obtained. Figure 8.2 shows
the percentage of time spent by MOEW on the different functions for
the three datasets. It can be appreciated that the FNDS method time
becomes a significant bottleneck of the procedure, as expected.
8.2.2
Solving the bottleneck via a multi-population approach
After confirming that the FNDS method of NSGA-II is a critical bottle-
neck of MOEW when dealing with high-dimensional FS problems, this
section shows how SMP-MOEW, a multi-population implementation
of MOEW proposed in Section 5.3, reduces its execution time by a
factor of nsp, confirming Hypothesis H1. In this case, only subject 104
from the Essex EEG datasets described in Appendix B.2 is used for the
experiment. The reasons for this are:
• All Essex datasets have the same dimensionality (356 samples
and 3 600 features).
• As shown in Section 8.2, the percentage of time spent on the
FNDS method analyzing each dataset is similar.

8.5
conclusions
This chapter has presented the results to validate the different wrapper
optimizations proposed in Chapter 5 to address Objective O2. Specif-
ically, the Elitist Probabilistic policy presented in Section 5.2 has been


142
8 moew optimizations efficiency
validated against the classical policies and confirmed to be the best
option when considering the average test Kappa index, the average
number of features, and the number of migrants selected. Then, the
bottleneck of the NSGA-II’s FNDS method when addressing high-
dimensional FS problems has been quantified, and its impact has been
reduced thanks to the distribution of individuals into subpopulations,
which was achieved by SMP-MOEW, a multi-population model of
MOEW. Next, the high efficiency achieved by PMP-MOEW, a parallel
version of SMP-MOEW, has been verified, as expected. Finally, the
results related to the optimization of hyperparameter p f has revealed
that, as postulated in Hypothesis H2, a decrease in its value leads to
a reduction of the generations needed to converge. However, it seems
that the optimal value of p f is not always lower than the commonly
used 0.5 since for the Isolet5 dataset a p f of 0.63 has been obtained.
The discussion and interpretation of all these results can be found in
Section 10.2.
With this in mind, the following chapter presents the experimental
results related to the optimization of the wrapper migration hyperpa-
rameters for high-dimensional FS problems (Objective O3).

statistical tests described in Section 6.4, as this is a value commonly

9.3 determination of the optimal population partitioning scheme

9.3
determination of the optimal population partition-
ing scheme
According to the analysis in the previous section, the size of sub-
populations seems to be a critical factor in multi-population models.
Therefore, the next step is to determine the optimal population parti-
tioning scheme (nspmax, sspmin) that prevents the search from stalling at
local optima and also minimizes resource consumption, following the
methodology proposed in Section 6.5. In this sense, since the degrada-
tion of results has started to become more evident for scheme (16, 240)
and those with smaller subpopulation sizes, the value of sspmin should
probably be in the interval [240, 480], whose extremes are the subpop-
ulation sizes of successive schemes (16, 240) and (8, 480), the former
generating degraded results and the latter not. Therefore, this interval
has been explored with the binary search proposed in Algorithm 6.1
to find a value for sspmin that does not degrade the results. In addition,
the number of subpopulations has been set at 16, as suggested in Sec-
tion 6.5, since this is the number of subpopulations of scheme (16, 240),
the scheme that started to show noticeable degradation.
The remaining hyperparameters controlling the binary search were
set as follows. Regarding wth, which defines the minimum width of
the search interval to stop the search as described in Section 6.5, since
the total number of individuals is ni= 3 840, wth has been set to 50
to obtain an adequate trade-off between resource consumption and
the desired precision for sspmin. Finally, sth, the similarity threshold for
comparing scores (6.10) has been set to 0.05.

9.5
conclusions
This chapter has experimentally validated the methodology to adjust
the migration process to high-dimensional FS problems proposed in
Chapter 6 in response to Objective O3. First, the influence of the popu-
lation partitioning scheme on the behavior of PMP-MOEW has been
assessed, confirming that the subpopulation size is the key element in
the migration process, since PMP-MOEW converges prematurely with
low subpopulation sizes, as expected. Next, the issue of premature con-
vergence has been mitigated by determining an appropriate value of
sspmin for each dataset, which subsequently allowed the identification of
nspmax. Once the optimal population partitioning scheme (nspmax, sspmin)
was identified, the influence of mi and ml was determined, which, as
postulated in Hypothesis H3, was reduced to a matter of efficiency,
which improves for low mi and high ml values.
This chapter completes the presentation of the experimental results.
Therefore, the following part discusses them and concludes this disser-
tation.

10.1
development of a robust base wrapper
Objective O1 aimed to develop an EA-based multi-objective wrapper to
effectively address FS problems in high-dimensional spaces. This was a
critical undertaking because a robust procedure was needed to ensure
the success of subsequent objectives.
The effectiveness of MOEW was verified following the methodology
proposed in Section 4.5, which aims to compare the subsets of features
found by MOEW with those obtained by other state-of-the-art wrappers
using different datasets. Since it was not possible to find a set of
wrappers that analyzed all the proposed datasets, both for low and high
dimensionality, with comparable metrics, the analysis was performed
independently for each type of dimensionality.
With respect to the analysis of low-dimensional data, several datasets
from the UCI repository were analyzed. Table D.1 shows that MOEW
seems to achieve a better average test accuracy and manages to re-
duce the average number of selected features compared to the other
alternative wrappers in the majority of the datasets. This preliminary
conclusion was confirmed using the dominance operator introduced
in Section 4.5, which applies parametric and non-parametric tests to
perform a robust statistical analysis of the results of all wrapper al-

10.2
wrapper optimizations
Although MOEW has proven to be an effective solution for solving
high-dimensional FS problems, its efficiency still had considerable
room for improvement. In this sense, Objective O2 proposes a series of
optimizations, addressed in Chapter 5, to improve its efficiency. The
results achieved by these improvements, presented in Chapter 8, are
discussed below.
10.2.1
Development of a novel migration policy for multi-objective optimiza-
tion problems
As mentioned in Section 2.2.1.2, the best-worst policy seems to be the
most appropriate option for hyperparameter mp, since it increases the
selection pressure with the consequent acceleration of the algorithm
convergence. However, since this dissertation deals with MOOPs (see
Section 2.1.2), it was necessary to adapt this policy to this type of prob-
lem. In this context, the Elitist Probabilistic migration policy described
in Section 5.2 was proposed.
As shown in Section 8.1, the new proposed migration policy and the
best-worst policy obtain similar results for both the average test Kappa
index and the average number of selected features, which was expected
since both consider the best individuals in the population. In contrast, it
seems that the evolutionary procedure experienced a degradation in its
effectiveness when the random-random policy was used, which could be
due to the lack of elitism of the policy. Regardless of the effectiveness of
the procedure, it can also be seen that the number of migrants selected
by the Elitist Probabilistic policy was significantly reduced compared
to the other two strategies, as expected, from a fixed number of 60
migrants selected by both the best-worst and random-random policies to
about 10 migrants for the Elitist Probabilistic policy.
A robust comparison of the behavior of the wrapper according to the
≺r
d operator and based on the distributions of the average test Kappa
index, the average number of selected features, and the number of
migrants selected by SMP-MOEW was performed. Although the Elitist


166
10 discussion
Probabilistic migration policy and the best-worst policy achieve compa-
rable results for both objectives, the former selects significantly fewer
individuals, making the novel policy the best when all three metrics
are considered. On the other hand, the random-random policy achieves
results with a comparable average number of features, although it can-
not reach the average test Kappa index obtained by the elitist policies,
making it the worst option.
In light of the above considerations, it can be stated that the proposed
policy achieves appropriate solutions while minimizing the overhead
of the migration process, mainly due to the significant reduction in the
number of migrants, thus successfully fulfilling Objective O2.1.
10.2.2
Development of a sequential multi-population EA-based wrapper
The FNDS method of NSGA-II is expected to be a significant bottleneck
for high-dimensional FS problems, since its algorithmic complexity is
O(no · ni2) and ni is typically set to a value close to n f for FS problems
(see Section 2.1.8). In this sense, the first step was to assess the relevance
of this bottleneck by addressing real high-dimensional datasets. Specifi-
cally, the datasets generated by the BCI lab at the University of Essex for
subjects 104, 107, and 110 were analyzed. As shown in Figure 8.2, the
percentage of execution time spent on the FNDS method of NSGA-II
exceeds 50%, leaving the evaluation of solutions as a secondary issue,
which is rather surprising since the evaluation of individuals has histor-
ically been considered the main bottleneck in EAs, as discussed in [293].
Thus, it is empirically confirmed that the non-dominated sorting of
individuals performed by NSGA-II is a major challenge when dealing
with high-dimensional FS problems.
This bottleneck is alleviated by SMP-MOEW, a multi-population model
of MOEW presented in Section 5.3 to address Objective O2.2. In fact,
Figure 8.3 shows a linear speedup for NSGA-II’s FNDS method as indi-
viduals are distributed into an increasing number of subpopulations.
Furthermore, Figure 8.4 illustrates how the non-dominated sorting
time becomes practically negligible as the number of subpopulations
increases, leaving the evaluation method as the only bottleneck of
the procedure. Nevertheless, the percentage devoted to the remain-
ing SMP-MOEW functions also increases slightly, mainly due to the
increment in the number of migrations as the number of subpopula-
tions increases. Finally, although SMP-MOEW still runs sequentially, it
achieves a speedup of almost ×2.5 just by partitioning individuals into


10.2 wrapper optimizations
167
subpopulations, thanks to the reduction in the time spent on the FNDS
method.
Considering the above, the results have validated Hypothesis H1, thus
confirming the successful achievement of Objective O2.2.
10.2.3
Parallelization of the multi-population EA-based wrapper
Since each subpopulation of SMP-MOEW evolves independently, ex-
cept for the migration process, it could be executed on a different
CPU core to make the wrapper more efficient. Thus, PMP-MOEW, the
parallel version of SMP-MOEW, was introduced in Section 5.4 to ad-
dress Objective O2.3. In addition, PMP-MOEW performs asynchronous
migrations so that slower populations do not stall faster ones.
The experimental results presented in Section 8.3 show the great im-
provement in efficiency achieved by PMP-MOEW, thus satisfying Ob-
jective O2.3. In fact, a superlinear speedup is achieved. This can be ex-
plained by the alleviation of the FNDS bottleneck of NSGA-II achieved
by applying a multi-population model combined with the parallel exe-
cution of each subpopulation. Since PMP-MOEW aims to ensure that
all physical CPU cores used are compute-active most of the time, a
speedup close to nsp is expected in this respect. Add to this the fact
that the FNDS execution time is divided by a factor of nsp, and this
behavior is explained. Specifically, the speedup is about ×35 with 24
subpopulations. In terms of power consumption, the saving is less
than the speedup in execution time, because the larger the number of
subpopulations, the more cores are used in parallel, which leads to
a corresponding increase in power consumption. However, this does
not prevent a superlinear energy gain in all cases except when 24
subpopulations are used, which is a very favorable result.
10.2.4
Boosting the convergence of the EA-based wrapper by reducing the
average size of the individuals in the initial population
The final optimization proposed for MOEW is related to reducing the
average size of individuals in the initial population to boost conver-
gence (Hypothesis H2), which depends on the hyperparameter p f . A
binary search-based procedure was proposed to estimate the optimal
value of p f . It was applied to PMP-MOEW for efficiency reasons, and


168
10 discussion
the remaining hyperparameters of the wrapper were tuned through
a trial-and-error process. This procedure was applied to several high-
dimensional datasets to assess whether the value of p f is dataset depen-
dent, as hypothesized in Section 5.5. Specifically, the datasets generated
by the BCI laboratory at the University of Essex for subjects 104, 107,
and 110, and the Isolet5 and Lung Cancer datasets were analyzed (see
Appendix B).
The results presented in Section 8.4 show a clear correlation between a
reduction in the value of p f and a decrease in the number of generations
required to converge, confirming Hypothesis H2. Besides, Figure 8.7
shows that for the Isolet5 dataset, and especially for the Lung Cancer

selected features. This behavior is probably related to the methodol-
ogy used to generate the Lung Cancer dataset (see Appendix B.3),
which was obtained through a previous feature extraction process, thus
reducing its dimensionality and eliminating most of the noise.
Furthermore, Table 8.3 shows that the optimal value of p f depends on
the dataset, with significant variations in its value, as expected. For the
three Essex datasets, the most appropriate value of p f was 0.01. The
binary search tried the two extremes of the interval [0.01, 1] and found
statistically similar results for both the average test Kappa index and
the average number of features selected, stopping at the first iteration.
On the other hand, the binary search found a value for p f of 0.63 and
0.22 for the Isolet5 and Lung Cancer datasets, respectively, with the
former standing out because it is higher than the commonly used 0.5,
which is certainly unexpected. This fact raises the question of whether
the adjustment of this hyperparameter has been appropriate in the
literature so far.
Table 8.3 shows another notable result: the number of generations to
converge and the number of features selected by PMP-MOEW for the
Isolet5 dataset increased when using the optimal value of p f (0.63)
compared to the commonly used value of 0.5. It is expected that PMP-
MOEW will require more generations when individuals are initialized
with a higher number of selected features. However, this has not re-
sulted in a decrease in the performance of PMP-MOEW. Thanks to
the ≺r
d operator, it can be observed that PMP-MOEW with the op-

speed up PMP-MOEW. For the Essex datasets, speedups and energy

analysis of the migration hyperparameters influ-
ence on the wrapper behavior for high-dimensional
datasets
Objective O3 aimed to determine the influence of the most relevant
migration hyperparameters on the behavior of PMP-MOEW when
solving high-dimensional FS problems that require large populations
to adequately cover the search space (see Section 2.1.8). This should
confirm whether the guidelines proposed 20 years ago by authors
such as Cantú-Paz or Tomassini are still valid today, when both the
dimensionality of FS problems and the size of the population required
to solve them have increased significantly (Hypothesis H3). Specifically,
the methodology proposed in Chapter 6 was validated by analyzing
the three high-dimensional Essex FS datasets.
In particular, the hyperparameters mi, ml, and nsp were analyzed. Fol-
lowing Tanese’s guideline, all population partitioning schemes (nsp, ssp)
were determined according to the total number of individuals ni and
each possible value for nsp. In addition to the average test Kappa index
and the average number of selected features, execution time and energy
consumption were also considered.


170
10 discussion
10.3.1
Analysis of the influence of the population partitioning scheme
First, the influence of the population partitioning scheme (Objective
O3.1) was analyzed by performing a grid search over all possible combi-
nations of migration hyperparameters to analyze the dependence of the
premature convergence of the wrapper on the subpopulation size. The
methodology proposed in Section 6.3 was applied in Section 9.2 and
it was found that, for the three datasets, degradation starts to appear
when the total population is divided into 16 subpopulations of 240
individuals, and especially when it is divided into 24 subpopulations
of 160 individuals. This behavior is consistent with the conclusions
of Cantú-Paz in [151]. As the size of subpopulations decreases, the
wrapper tends to get stuck in local optima. In particular, it can be
observed that as ssp decreases due to an increase in nsp, a deterioration
of the average test Kappa index along with a decrease in the average
number of selected features confirms that PMP-MOEW has an increas-
ing tendency to converge prematurely to local optima, validating the
method proposed in Section 6.3.
10.3.2
Optimization of the population partitioning scheme
Once it was determined that premature convergence occurred between
population partitioning schemes (16, 240) and (8, 480), the threshold
for the minimum subpopulation size sspmin should be in the interval
[240, 480], as hypothesized in Section 6.5. Therefore, the binary search
procedure proposed in Algorithm 6.1 was applied to the three datasets
to estimate it. Section 9.3 showed that subpopulation sizes equal to
or greater than 300 individuals, which is about 10% of the total pop-
ulation, effectively addressed the problem of premature convergence
for the three datasets, underscoring the importance of adjusting the
subpopulation size appropriately.
After replacing the subpopulation size sspj of all population partition-
ing schemes suffering from premature convergence with sspmin, the
maximum threshold for the number of subpopulations, nspmax, was de-
termined. Figure 9.9 shows that using 16 subpopulations yields results
comparable to those using 24, but is more computationally efficient,
i.e., nspmax = 16, and thus (nspmax, sspmin) is the optimal population
partitioning scheme for the problem (Objective O3.2), validating the
methodology proposed in Section 6.5. A priori, this behavior may be
unexpected, as it has been assumed over the years that increasing the
number of subpopulations is the best guideline to follow [96, 294, 295].


10.3 analysis of the migration hyperparameters influence
171
However, it seems that once the problem of premature convergence is
avoided by setting ssp ≥sspmin, values of nsp > nspmax do not improve
the results obtained, although they do require more computational
resources.
10.3.3
Analysis of the influence of the remaining of migration hyperparame-
ters
The optimal population partitioning scheme identified for the three
datasets was used to analyze the influence of mi and ml on the behav-
ior of PMP-MOEW (Objective O3.3). In this sense, Section 9.4 shows
that both hyperparameters only affect its efficiency. In particular, the
procedure converges faster as mi decreases and ml increases. This may
contradict the guidelines given by Tomassini [155], who recommended
using average values for both hyperparameters. In fact, Tomassini
reported a degradation in the quality of the solutions when these hy-
perparameters were tuned in this way. Perhaps this degradation could
have been avoided by properly tuning nsp and ssp.
Finally, after determining the appropriate values for the migration
hyperparameters, it is worth noting that their values are consistent
with those obtained through the trial-and-error process carried out
to hyperparametrize the wrapper to validate the Elitist Probabilistic
migration policy and optimize p f . This fact confirms the methodology
proposed in Chapter 6, which allows to fine-tune the migration process
for high-dimensional FS problems.
10.3.4
The novel ranking-based score as a metric to estimate both statistical
similarity and effect size
The ranking-based score developed in Section 6.4 allowed for multi-
ple comparisons of the result sample distributions obtained with 140
different hyperparameterizations of the wrapper across three different
datasets, which was key to fine-tuning the migration process. Further-
more, it was also found that both the absolute difference in scores and
the Cohen’s d index, which estimates the effect size, appeared to follow
the same trends for the three Essex datasets. Therefore, the Pearson
coefficient has been calculated to estimate the correlation between the
absolute difference in scores and the Cohen’s d index for all cases and


172

all datasets to confirm whether the absolute difference in scores could
be used to estimate the effect size.
Regarding the study of the influence of the population partitioning
scheme on the premature convergence of the wrapper performed in
Section 9.2, the Pearson coefficient values for the correlation between
the absolute difference of the scores and the effect size for subjects 104,
107, and 110, are 0.659, 0.850, and 0.935 for the average test Kappa index
(Figures 9.2 and 9.3) and 0.795, 0.538, and 0.728 for the average number

These results support the hypothesis that the new score metric intro-

and the magnitude of such differences. This gives the new score enor-

statistical studies, which, as discussed in Section 2.6, are fundamental
for comparing the behavior of stochastic procedures.
10.3.5
Magnitude of the experimental study
It is worth mentioning the extent of the experimental study conducted
to obtain the results presented in Chapter 9. The relationship between
the population partitioning scheme and the likelihood of premature
convergence was confirmed by applying PMP-MOEW to three high-
dimensional datasets, using five population partitioning schemes, four
values for the migration interval, and seven values for ml. Each different
combination of these hyperparameters was used to run PMP-MOEW
30 times, resulting in 12 600 runs of the wrapper. In addition, the
binary search used to estimate the optimal population partitioning
scheme tried another four additional population partitioning schemes,
requiring 10 080 runs. Finally the validation of the optimal population
partitioning scheme required another 2 520 runs of PMP-MOEW. Thus,
the experimental part of this work alone took more than a year to
complete, despite the use of six high-performance computing nodes.

11.1
main contributions
The main contributions of this thesis are:
1. A base wrapper (MOEW) that successfully tackles low-, medium-,
and high-dimensional FS problems, competitively matching or
even improving the results of other state-of-the-art wrappers.
2. A dominance criterion supporting multiple performance metrics
that facilitates statistical comparison between two result sample
distributions obtained by two different wrapper alternatives.
3. A new version of the best-worst migration policy for MOOPs, the
Elitist Probabilistic migration, which selects the best migrants from
the Pareto front according to the new hyperparameter ml.
4. Although it has been assumed in the past that solution evaluation
is the main bottleneck of an EA-based wrapper, the fact is that
NSGA-II’s FNDS method creates an even more severe bottleneck.
Therefore, a multi-population version of MOEW (SMP-MOEW) is
proposed, which effectively mitigates the NSGA-II’s FNDS issue
by partitioning individuals into subpopulations. In particular, the
time required for this method is reduced by a factor of nsp.
5. A parallel wrapper for UMA architectures, PMP-MOEW, that
evolves each subpopulation independently on a different CPU
core and exchanges migrants asynchronously to prevent slower
subpopulations from stalling the execution flow of faster ones.
6. Confirmation that the average size of individuals in the initial
population, controlled by the hyperparameter p f , affects the con-
vergence of an evolutionary process.
7. A method for finding the optimal value of p f that boosts the
convergence of EA-based wrappers.
8. A new score metric, supported by parametric and non-parametric
statistical tests, that can separate different hyperparameterizations
of an EA-based wrapper into clusters with statistically similar
results, and assign each cluster a scalar score according to a given
metric, allowing complete ordering of the clusters.
9. Confirmation that the absolute difference between the score val-
ues of a wrapper behavior metric for two different hyperparame-


11.2 future work
177
terizations correlates with the effect size of their results, estimated
by the Cohen’s d index. This finding facilitates the statistical com-
parison of results for different hyperparametrizations, since the
new score metric can be used to detect statistically significant
differences in the results of two hyperparametrizations, and also
to estimate the effect size of such differences.
10. The size of the subpopulations appears to be the key factor in
properly adjusting migrations. Regardless of the problem, there
seems to be a minimum threshold for the subpopulations size
below which the multi-population evolutionary model tends to
converge prematurely. Population sizes above this threshold pro-
duce statistically similar results. Thus, this minimum threshold
can be considered the optimal subpopulation size.
11. A method for finding the optimal subpopulation size for a given
problem. This method also provides a maximum threshold for
the number of subpopulations, thereby obtaining the optimal
population partitioning scheme for a given problem, in which
optimal is defined as the one that produces the best results with
the least amount of computation. This finding contradicts classical
recommendations, which assume that results improve as the
number of subpopulations increases.
12. The number of migrants and the migration interval do not affect
the efficacy of the wrapper once the optimal population parti-
tioning scheme is used. They only affect the efficiency of the
procedure, which improves as the number of migrants increases
and the migration interval decreases.
11.2
future work
The field of bioinformatics is poised for significant growth, with op-
portunities for progress on multiple fronts. This dissertation advances
the effectiveness and efficiency of evolutionary wrappers for high-
dimensional FS problems, the results of which have been published in
relevant papers. However, there is still room for further work in line
with the developed methods.
The proposed multi-population model (SMP-MOEW) addresses the
significant limitation of NSGA-II’s FNDS method for high-dimensional
FS problems, providing a solution to this critical bottleneck. However,
further work is required to address the other bottleneck shown in


178
11 conclusions and future fork
Section 8.2.2, namely the evaluation of potential solutions with the k-
NN classifier. Once the individuals are divided into 24 subpopulations
and the FNDS bottleneck of NSGA-II is mitigated, k-NN accounts for
almost 90% of the execution time for dataset 104. Therefore, exploring
the potential of coprocessors, such as GPUs, to improve the efficiency
of k-NN would be a valuable avenue to pursue.
Although PMP-MOEW achieved a superlinear gain and significantly
improved its efficiency, other parallelization strategies could be applied,
such as distributing PMP-MOEW to take advantage of all the nodes
of a distributed system. In this way, even larger FS problems could be
tackled.
Finally, at the end of the development of this thesis, the new version
of Python (3.13) was released, which allows users to disable the GIL.
Therefore, the use of threads instead of processes to support PMP-
MOEW should be analyzed.

Three high-dimensional datasets generated by the BCI Laboratory at
the University of Essex, corresponding to three human subjects, coded
104, 107, and 110. They consist of signals, called EEGs, corresponding
to three different types of imaginated movement: left hand, right hand,
and feet. The procedure for recording the EEGs, as described in [298],
follows the typical protocol of a cue-based approach, with the subject
seated in a chair approximately 1.5 m from the screen. On each trial,
the subject experiences the following sequence presented on the screen:
1. Blank screen. The subject has between 2.5 - 3.5 seconds to relax
and prepare for the next trial.
2. Fixation cross. At instant t = 0 and for 2 seconds, a fixation cross
appears on the screen to indicate that the trial is about to begin.
3. Visual cue. In addition to the fixation cross, a visual cue indicating
the start of the trial is displayed for 6 seconds at t = 2. An
auditory cue is also emitted at t = 2. The relative position of the
cue with respect to the fixation cross indicates the type of MI that
MI: Motor Imagery
the subject must perform: down for the foot movements and right
or left for the corresponding hand movements.


186
b datasets information
Each recording session is divided into four runs, providing a total
of 356 samples, of which the first 178 are used for training and the
remaining 178 for testing. EEGs are acquired from 32 electrodes at
256 Hz using the BioSemi system [300] and processed using the MRA
MRA: MultiResolu-
tion Analysis
method, although only 15 of the 32 electrodes are ultimately usable.
Since a trial is recorded from the fixation cross to the end of the cue,
an EEG contains 256 × 8 = 2 048 samples per channel. The resulting
signal is composed of multiple segments characterized by a set of
details and approximation coefficients belonging to different levels of
wavelets [301]. Generalizing, each dataset is defined by 15 electrodes,
20 segments, 6 wavelet levels, and 2 details/coefficients. In total, there
are 15 × 20 × 6 × 2 = 3 600 sets of coefficients with sizes ranging from
4 to 128. In addition, as shown in [298], the number of coefficients
is reduced to only 3 600 by computing the second moment of the
coefficient distribution (variance) for each set and normalizing the
obtained value to the interval (0, 1). In summary, both the training and
test datasets of the three subjects are composed of 178 signals with
3 600 features each.
b.3
lung cancer
The lung cancer dataset was collected from the ACC and SCC projects
ACC: AdenoCarCi-
noma
SCC: Squamous Cell
Carcinoma
of the TCGA database [299]. To provide more context, the signs and
symptoms of ACC are similar to other forms of lung cancer, and
patients most commonly complain of persistent cough and shortness
of breath. ACC is more common in patients with a history of cigarette
smoking and is the most common form of lung cancer in younger
women and Asian populations [302]. Otherwise, SCC originates in the
bronchi and is strongly associated with tobacco smoking. It is also the
second most common type of lung cancer after ACC.
After providing an overview of the data source, it is important to em-
phasize that only transcriptomic characterization files were considered.
The number of selected samples is 489 from ACC, 498 from SCC, and
103 control samples from both projects, for a total of 1 090 samples.
All TCGA samples are harmonized according to the same protocols to
avoid bias and normalization issues. Both gene expression extraction
and sample harmonization procedures are described in [303].
Each transcriptomic file could contain the gene expression values of
more than 25 000 genes, more than 90% of which do not show signif-
icant differences between the considered groups. For this reason, the
multiclass DEGs extraction procedure proposed in [277] was applied
DEG: Differential
Expressed Genes


b.3 lung cancer
187
to pre-filter nonsense genes, which allows the detection of DEGs that
are differentially expressed in different classes by counting the number
of biclass comparisons in which this differential expression occurs,
resulting in a total of 410 DEGs (features).

200
e basic use of the main python libraries
e.1
deap
The DEAP library provides all the necessary tools for developing EAs
in Python. Although its complete documentation can be found in [304],
a description of the Base [305] and Creator [306] modules would be
helpful to understand the source code of the procedures developed in
this dissertation.
On the one hand, the Base module provides the basic structures and
components necessary for the development of different parts of an EA,
including the base.Toolbox and base.Fitness classes. The former allows the
registration of any type of operator or function, whether proprietary
to DEAP or user-developed, for use within the code. The base.Fitness
serves as a tool to define the type of objective function associated
with the EA. On the other hand, the Creator module is a meta-factory
that allows the generation of classes. Therefore, the fitness of the base
wrapper (MOEW) is defined as follows:
creator.create("Fitness", base.Fitness, weights=(1.0, -1.0))
The first argument of the create function is simply the name assigned
to the new fitness function. The second argument represents the class
to inherit from, in this case the fitness function of the Base module. The
third argument specifies the attributes to add to the instantiation of
that class, which in this context is the optimization objective. A value
of 1.0 indicates a maximization objective (classifier effectiveness), while
a value of −1.0 indicates a minimization objective (number of features
selected). In DEAP, individuals have an attribute called fitness.values
(tuple format), and it is the developer’s responsibility to assign a value
to this attribute when evaluating the individual. Now that the fitness
function has been specified, the individual is defined as follows:
creator.create("Individual", np.ndarray, fitness = creator.Fitness)
The fitness function described above is used as an attribute of the
class chosen for the individuals. Since an integer subset of feature
indices is chosen to represent individuals in this dissertation, the class
numpy.array from the Numpy library is used to store these indices
because, as described in Section 2.4.2, this library is written internally
in C and its execution is highly efficient.


e.2 scikit-learn
201
Finally, the base.Toolbox class is used as follows to register the wrapper
components:
toolbox.register("selectNSGA2", tools.selNSGA2)
The argument list is similar to that of the create function mentioned
earlier, except that the second argument refers to a function instead of
a class. This function can be a DEAP-specific function [307], such as
the NSGA-II selection function included in DEAP and illustrated in the
example, or an external function developed specifically for the code, as
is the case with MOEW’s crossover and mutation operators. The third
argument (if any) represents the parameters of the function.
e.2
scikit-learn
Since Scikit-learn provides a variety of tools for ML, both its k-NN imple-
mentation and the Kappa index calculation are used in the wrapper’s
evaluation function. The k-NN model [218] in Scikit-learn is generated
by the following statement:
model = KNeighborsClassifier(n_neighbors = value, algorithm=’brute’)
The syntax is straightforward, with the first argument specifying the
value of k and the second the algorithm used. As discussed in Sec-
tion 4.3.2.1, brute-force k-NN was chosen. The model is then trained
with the following instruction:
model.fit(data_train, labels_train)
Finally, the test Kappa index is obtained with the following Scikit-learn
statement, using the predict function that forecasts the labels of the test
data:
cohen_kappa_score(model.predict(data_test), labels_test)


202
e basic use of the main python libraries
e.3
multiprocessing
This Python library is designed to facilitate process-based parallelism.
As a tutorial, each of the functions presented here are applied to the
efficient parallel wrapper (PMP-MOEW) presented in Section 5.4. In
this sense, the Process class can be used as follows:
proc = Process(target=function, args=(arg1, arg2, arg3))
The first argument is the function called by the subprocess, which for
PMP-MOEW is the function that executes the NSGA-II code, while the
second argument is a tuple containing the parameters of the function.
This sentence is executed as many times as the number of subpopu-
lations, allowing the library to associate each subprocess with a CPU
core.
Once the subprocesses are created, each one can be executed with the
following statement:
proc.start()
Each subprocess handles a different subpopulation when MOEW runs,
exchanging individuals only during the migration process. While this
statement executes all of the function’s code, the various subprocesses
should be properly terminated. The following statement is used to
terminate a process:
proc.terminate()
As discussed in Section 5.4.1.1, the Queue class from the Multiprocessing
library was used to support the asynchronous migration process. A
new Queue instance can be created with the following statement:
multiprocessing.Queue()
The function that allows non-blocking placement of items in the queue
is:


e.3 multiprocessing
203
put_nowait()
In contrast, the function that provides the mechanism to asynchronously
retrieve items from a queue is:
get_nowait()
Finally, the status of the queue (whether it is empty or not) is checked
using the following function, which returns true if the queue is empty
or false otherwise:
empty()
